activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Molar mass in grams per mole has the same number as a particle's average mass in atomic mass units; one carbon atom averages about 12.01 units, and one mole of carbon about 12.01 grams.
story:
The night before the chemistry retake, Samantha spread her notes across the kitchen table while her mother washed dishes behind her, ostentatiously quiet. She had until eight the next morning to learn what she had failed in June: grams of one thing, moles of another. On paper it looked like nothing, four lines of arithmetic, and yet in June she had watched the numbers slide apart in her hands and written something confident and wrong.

Eleonore arrived first, carrying a supermarket bag of energy drinks she set down without comment, the way you leave flowers at a door. Fabrice came ten minutes later, still in his work shirt, apologizing for a shift that had run long. He had passed the exam the first time, though not well, and Samantha suspected he had come mostly so she would not have to be alone with it.

The problem she chose to start with was one from the old test: given so many grams of carbon, how many moles of the product form. She copied the numbers onto a fresh sheet, and there it was, 12.01, sitting in the periodic table square beside the letter C. She had copied that square a hundred times in her life, for flashcards, for the cover of a lab notebook, and never once looked at it properly.

"Wait," she said. "This 12.01. That's the mass of one atom, right? One carbon atom weighs about 12.01 of those tiny units." She tapped the table.

Eleonore leaned over, chewing the inside of her cheek. "That's what the little square means, I think. Average mass of one atom."

"And then here, in my notes from Mr. Mansour, the molar mass of carbon is 12.01 grams per mole." Samantha put her finger under the second number, then under the first. "Same number. One atom is about 12.01 atomic mass units, and a whole mole of it is 12.01 grams." She said it twice in her head, testing it for the trick she assumed must be hiding in it, the way the class had once hidden an oligarchy of three boys who decided the lab groups and called it consensus. But the numbers just sat there, matching, and the matching, when she let it, felt less like a trick than like a door left open on purpose.

"So which one do I use for this problem?" Fabrice asked, hovering his pen. "The atom one or the mole one?"

"That's the thing. They're the same number, so for the arithmetic it doesn't matter which face you look at. The grams you're given, divided by 12.01 grams per mole, gives you moles of carbon." She worked it through, then carried the moles across the balanced equation to the product side, multiplying by the ratio, and there was the answer, clean and ordinary as a coin. She checked it against the marking scheme Eleonore had photocopied at the library and collated into a stack with the questions in order. It matched.

They did three more, one after another, and Fabrice got one wrong by forgetting the ratio, and Eleonore found his error before Samantha did and slid the paper back to him without a word of triumph. Somewhere past eleven Samantha's mother set out bread and cheese and three glasses of milk, having decided, apparently, that teenagers studying in her kitchen were her business whether or not they said so. Eleonore thanked her in French, which made her linger, pleased.

What Samantha could not settle, even as the problems yielded, was why nobody had ever told her the two numbers matched, or whether the matching was a coincidence of the sort she should simply be grateful for. Mr. Mansour had written the molar mass on the board every single lesson; the atomic mass had been in the textbook's inside cover. She had assumed the two facts lived in separate rooms, one for enormous things and one for invisible ones, and it unsettled her a little to find the wall between them had been a curtain all along. Maybe that was the actual lesson, or maybe there was a reason behind it that would arrive in some later course, in some later year, the way most true things seemed to arrive for her, late and obvious in retrospect.

Fabrice left at half past one with the canny suggestion that she sleep with the formulas under her pillow, and Eleonore stayed to wash the glasses so Samantha's mother would not have to. Samantha sat on alone in the kitchen with the periodic table, tracing the column of small numbers downward, checking each element the way you check a lock before bed. At the window the sky was beginning to gray at the edge, and on the table the last problem waited, unsolved, its blank answer line catching the light of the lamp.

She picked up her pen.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A digital elevation model is a raster layer storing the ground height of each cell, which GIS uses to predict where water will flow and collect.
story:
The rain had stopped by the time Ms. Cohen called them out of the vans, but the river below the campsite ran brown and fast, and Jason stood at the edge of the gravel bar watching a submerged branch shudder in the current. He had his father's laptop under his arm in a dry bag, which felt absurd in the middle of a state park, except that the whole reason for the trip was the competition, and the competition was in thirty-one hours.

"Screen's going to be hard to read out here," Sylvie said, dropping her pack beside his.

"I brought the clearing." He nodded toward the flat ground near the fire ring. "And a hooded sweatshirt as a glare shield."

Ms. Cohen had proposed the weekend herself: three of them, one project, no signal, one power bank rationed like water. Their entry for the state mapping challenge had to overlay flood risk on housing for the city of Alder Falls, and their first draft had gone to her in April looking, in her word, decorative. Colors, census tracts, a river drawn blue and confident as a lie.

Jason set up while Faith gathered firewood. He opened the project and there it was again, the problem that had bothered him since the draft: streets a half mile from the river, well outside anything you would call a floodplain, shaded the same risk red as the riverbank itself. He had assumed the data was wrong. The shapefile had come from a county portal, and county portals, he had told Sylvie, were where accuracy went to die.

"That's the river layer?" Faith asked, leaning over his shoulder, smelling of pine sap. Below his cursor the turbid water in the actual gorge had nothing to do with the tidy blue line on screen.

"It's everything. Flood risk, parcels, all of it. Look at Delancey Street." He zoomed. "Nowhere near the water. Still red. Sylvie, come look at this before it gets dark."

Sylvie came with an armload of wood and her own theory, which she delivered while crouched to build the fire. "They probably ascribe risk by neighborhood. Insurance companies do it. Redline the whole census tract and go to lunch."

"That's not science, that's gossip with a legend."

"Fine. Prove it's not that."

The light was going. Ms. Cohen walked past on her way to hang the food bag and paused, and Jason expected her to settle it, because she always settled things, but she only said, "What layer haven't you turned on?" and kept walking with the bear canister swinging from her hand.

He sat with that. He clicked through the layer list and found one he had never opened, labeled DEM, and underneath it, in the metadata, the words digital elevation model. "What's a DEM?" Faith asked. "Digital elevation model," Sylvie read off the screen. "It stores the ground height of every cell."

"It's a raster," Jason said slowly, turning it on, and the map changed under his hands. The city stopped being colors and became terrain, each square cell of ground holding its own height in shades of green and brown, and when he draped the flood layer over it the red on Delancey Street stopped looking arbitrary. The street sat in a low cell, a shallow bowl of ground rising away on three sides, and the model had drawn the water going where water goes. He pulled up the flow accumulation, and the map predicted it: rain collecting, moving downslope cell by cell, pooling exactly where the red was darkest.

"It's not about distance to the river," he said. "It never was. It's where the ground lets water collect."

Sylvie crossed her arms and looked at it for a long moment, firelight and screen light fighting on her face. "So I was going to make us write a paragraph about discriminatory redlining."

"You weren't wrong to ask. But it's not the answer here."

"I want it in the presentation anyway. One slide. Because the housing data is still true, Jason. The low ground is where the cheap parcels are, and that's not an accident, and a map that shows water without showing who lives in the water's path is a lie by omission."

"That's two arguments."

"That's one argument with two layers." She tapped the screen. "Overlay them. Isn't that the whole point of what we're doing?"

He had come out here, he realized, ready to defend the draft as a technical problem with a technical answer, and now the technical answer was sitting on his screen and it was not enough. The elevation model told you where the water would collect. It said nothing about why the low cells held the oldest public housing and the newest trailer court and none of the city council members' addresses. He thought about the word Sylvie used, ascribe, and how careful you had to be with it, because the model ascribed risk to cells of ground, and people ascribed everything else.

"Jason." Faith was holding out a pot of river water they had carried up for boiling, and it had gone turbid again, silt swirling where it had begun to settle. "If we're working past dark we eat first."

"Two slides," he said to Sylvie. "Yours after mine, so the water makes sense first. But I get to say what we don't know. The model's cells are ten meters, that's not fine enough to trust for a single lot, and I'm not going to stand up there and pretend it is."

"Deal."

They ate noodles by the fire, and afterward Ms. Cohen came back from the tree line and looked at the laptop over his shoulder, at the terrain glowing faint and green in the dark, at Delancey Street sitting in its bowl of low cells with the water predicted to come. She was quiet long enough that Faith started cleaning the pot.

"Well?" Jason said.

"Turn the brightness down," Ms. Cohen said. "You'll kill the battery."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Deliberate practice means working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, which improves skill more than simply playing through pieces already known.
story:
The violin had belonged to Daniel's grandfather, and for the first week at the house Daniel treated it like a museum piece, lifting it from its case with both hands and setting it down again. Then he found a beginner's book in the side table drawer, a pencil stub beside it, and by the fourth evening he could scratch his way through the whole of "Ode to Joy." He played it eleven times that night. The twelfth time, his grandfather looked up from his crossword.

"You know it now," his grandfather said. "So what are you practicing?"

Daniel lowered the bow. "It's the only song I have."

"You have the whole book."

The next afternoon Daniel played "Ode to Joy" another fifteen times, because it felt like being good at something, and being good at something felt rare that summer. On the shelf above the piano he had noticed a row of his grandfather's old books, and one evening, restless, he took down a thin volume about musicians and how they got that way. He read a chapter sitting on the porch steps while the sprinkler ticked across the neighbour's lawn. The chapter said that deliberate practice meant working on specific weaknesses with a clear goal and immediate feedback, and that this improved skill more than simply playing through pieces already known. He read the sentence twice, then looked back through the screen door at the violin case lying open on the sofa.

He called Katelyn, who had been playing cello since she was seven. When he described what he'd read, she laughed, not unkindly.

"It's called deliberate practice," she said. "My teacher hammers it. I used to hate it. Still do, honestly."

"How does the feedback part work if nobody's listening?"

"Record yourself. Phone's fine. You'll hear the wrong notes before the phone's even stopped."

The following morning Daniel set a goal before he touched the instrument: measures nineteen and twenty, the two bars where his second finger kept landing flat and the string change always smeared. He recorded the two bars on his phone, listened, winced, adjusted, recorded again. The notes came back to him with an immediacy that his own ears, busy with producing the sound, had never managed. He did this perhaps forty times, and the two bars did not become easy, but they became true, and the difference was audible even to him. When his grandfather drifted in with his coffee, Daniel played the passage once, cleanly.

"Better," his grandfather said, and sat down in the armchair. "Now the other part."

"There's another part?"

"The part after it. The part you've never once played."

Daniel hadn't thought about that. The book in his lap, and the summer, had felt almost grandiose in his imagination, a vision of himself transformed by September, walking into orchestra auditions with secret fluency. The reality was this: two bars, forty repetitions, a phone full of recordings he was slightly ashamed to keep. He thought about his father, who had quit piano at thirteen and still spoke of it with a flinch, who claimed he'd had no talent as though talent were a diagnosis. Daniel had half believed him. It was a comfortable belief, actually. It let you play "Ode to Joy" fifteen times and call it an afternoon.

He worked the next passage the same way, though it fought him longer, and by the end of the week the book's logic had begun to ossify into routine: pick the weak bars, name the goal, record, listen, correct. Routine, he noticed, was quieter than inspiration. Nobody claps for a correct string crossing. His grandfather listened from the armchair most evenings now, saying almost nothing, but when Daniel dragged the bow across a note that was genuinely wrong, the old man's hand would rise off the armrest before the sound had finished, a small immediate signal that Daniel had come to watch for out of the corner of his eye.

Roy came by on Saturday, having texted nothing, as usual, and stood in the doorway with two sodas. "You're still on that thing? I thought this was a phase."

"It's not a phase."

"Play something, then."

So Daniel played the two bars, then the four, then the eight, and it was a travesty of how the piece should sound, thin and cautious, nothing like a performance. But Roy, who had heard him scrape through "Ode to Joy" three weeks earlier, went quiet in a way that was its own kind of applause. After Roy left, Daniel sat on the porch with the violin across his knees, uncertain about plenty of things still, among them whether he would keep this up when school started and the evenings filled with other obligations. He only knew that the fifteen easy replays and the forty hard ones were not the same activity wearing two costumes, and that he could no longer pretend they were. He lifted the phone, set it recording, and set his fingers on the strings.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Hunter had the shoes on before he remembered he was supposed to be relaxed. The rental counter guy, a man with a name tag reading SOMSAK, waved him toward lane eleven, and Hunter walked over carrying the awkward brown-and-tan shoes like evidence of a crime. The whole alley hummed with that smell he could never place, floor wax and beer and the ghost of a thousand spilled sodas, and the scoreboard glowed above his lane with a cursor blinking next to a space for his name.

Jazmine arrived four minutes late, which he had already decided he would forgive her for, and then forgave her for again when she apologized twice before even picking up a ball. She wore a jacket with pins on it, little enameled things, a moth and a cassette tape, and he wanted to ask about every one of them and instead said, "You want to go first, or should I?"

"Rock paper scissors," she said, and beat him with scissors, and for the next forty minutes that was the high point of his performance, because he bowled badly. Not charmingly badly, either. Gutter-ball badly, in a way that sent his ball drifting right with an inevitability that seemed almost studied. She was decent, an easy swing and follow-through, and she laughed at herself when she got greedy and went for the ten pin and missed. He laughed at the right times. He thought he did. He could not be sure, because the problem with being seventeen is that you watch yourself from the outside the whole time, like a coach reviewing film that no one else will ever see.

Between frames they ate nachos, and Jazmine turned out to be an absolute epicure of the bowling alley snack bar, ordering the chili cheese fries with a seriousness usually reserved for wine lists. "The pretzels are a trap," she told him. "Sitting under that heat lamp for hours. But the fries, the fries have a system." He found this transfixing, the fact that she had a philosophy about it, that she had been here enough times to build one, and he asked her about the system until his turn came and he threw the ball directly into the gutter again.

At the end of the night they stood in the parking lot under an antiquated sign, half its letters dead so that it read S PLA, and he said, "This was fun," and heard how flat it came out, how much it sounded like a closing door. She said, "Yeah, it was," and then her mother's car pulled in and she said, "I'll text you," which everyone knows is a coin flip of a sentence. He watched the taillights go and began, immediately and without permission, to review the film.

He walked home because walking gave the review more room. He threw his own shoe. He had told a story about his uncle's parrot that had no ending, just a drift into silence. He had said "you too" when she said happy birthday, and his birthday was not for four months, and she had not said happy birthday, she had said happy Friday. There was the moment he asked about her pins and then interrupted her answer to apologize for interrupting. There was the entire nacho transaction in which he forgot his wallet was in his other pocket and stood patting himself like a man being frisked.

Keon was on his porch three houses down, because Keon was always on his porch, and he called out, "How was it," and Hunter sat heavily on the steps and said, "She tolerated it. She tolerated me. There were maybe two minutes where she seemed genuinely not bored."

"Okay, so, weird timing," Keon said. "We just covered this in psych. There's a study, Erica Boothby, 2018, and after a first conversation people underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. They call it the liking gap."

"Called it a gap," Hunter said. "Like a fact about geography."

"I'm telling you what the study found. Both people walked away thinking they did worse than the other person thought they did. Both people. Every time."

Hunter turned this over. He was aware that you could not simply download a fact into your chest and feel better, that knowing the brain skews one direction does not unskew it, and he said so, and Keon said, "Sure, but think about it from her side. She apologized twice for being four minutes late. To you. Who cares?" That stopped him, actually. She had apologized twice. She had shown him the fry system. She had beaten him at rock paper scissors and then done a small victory dance with her shoulders, a dance you do not do in front of someone whose opinion you don't care about.

His phone buzzed against his leg. He looked at it, then at Keon, then at it again, because on the screen was a message from Jazmine, and the message read: "ok full disclosure I was so nervous I put my ball in the gutter on purpose once so you wouldn't feel bad. also what's your favorite pin on my jacket, I couldn't tell if you were being polite or actually wanted to know. it's the moth."

Hunter read it twice. So the film had two cameras after all, and the second one had been pointed at her the whole time, recording a different movie: a girl so rattled she sabotaged her own score. He laughed, once, out loud into the dark street, at himself, at the both of them, at the gap that had apparently been standing in the parking lot between them like a third person neither of them introduced.

He still did not know if she liked him or if she was being kind or if kindness and liking were even different things here, and he decided, in the honest part of his head, that he did not get to know that tonight, maybe not for a while, maybe that was the whole arrangement. He typed, deleted, typed again.

"It's the moth," he wrote back. "Rematch Saturday. I'm bringing my own fries money and a better parrot story. It has an ending, I just panicked."

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: A lease that says 'utilities included' may cover only some utilities; the lease wording decides which, so each utility has to be checked separately.
story:
Thomas spread the two leases across the kitchen table after dinner, weighting the corners with the salt shaker and his mother's mug of cold tea. His mother was moving to the city in the fall for a hospital job, and she had asked him, almost as a joke, to be the one who read the fine print, since he was "the math person" in the house. It hadn't felt like a joke when he said yes.

The first apartment, on Alder Street, advertised eleven fifty a month, utilities included. The second, on Rosemont, was nine ninety with utilities listed separately. He had assumed, when he first saw the listings, that Alder Street was simply the more expensive place and that the whole question would take ten minutes. His mother had smiled at that and said she'd been assuming things about leases for twenty years and had paid for most of them.

He read the Alder lease slowly, the way Mr. Khoury, his old neighbor, had once told him to read contracts, "like the words are trying to get away from you." In the section on utilities, the lease said water and heat included. He looked for electricity and found it under a different heading, tenant responsibility, in a paragraph so short it seemed embarrassed of itself. He sat back. The phrase on the listing, utilities included, had captivated him more than any detail of the apartment itself, the bay window, the little balcony, and now he understood that the phrase had done exactly the work it was designed to do.

He texted Kohen, who had moved out of his own house at seventeen and now rented a room above a laundromat. Kohen replied within a minute: "lol yeah. utilities included never means all of them. you have to check each one, water, heat, electric, whatever. the lease wording is the only thing that counts." Then: "learned that the hard way, my december bill was a horror movie."

Thomas pulled a legal pad toward him and began a grid. Alder Street: eleven fifty, water and heat included, electricity separate. Rosemont: nine ninety, everything separate. He called the electric company and waited on hold for nineteen minutes, watching the light move across the table, while his mother dried dishes with her back to him so he wouldn't feel watched. When the agent finally answered, she gave him an average monthly figure for a one-bedroom in each neighborhood. He wrote the numbers in careful columns, then added garbage fees and renter's insurance, which Kohen had insisted on with the fervor of a convert.

The totals landed closer than he'd expected. Alder came out about forty dollars more per month, all-in. But the electricity estimate was just that, an estimate, and he didn't know whether the Alder Street unit was on the top floor under a sun-baked roof or whether Rosemont's ancient boiler would swallow every dollar the lower rent saved. He wrote "uncertainty" in the margin and underlined it twice, which made him feel slightly ridiculous, and then left it underlined anyway.

When his mother came to look, he walked her through the grid line by line. She leaned on the back of his chair, reading slowly, and he could feel her attention like a hand on his shoulder. "So the cheaper one isn't cheaper," she said.

"It might be. It's forty dollars apart and I can't promise the electricity number. That's the part I can't know from here." He tapped the margin. "But Alder's listing is misleading on purpose, and that tells you something about who you'd be renting from."

She laughed, a short, tectonic shift in her whole frame, the tiredness rearranging itself into something lighter. "Twenty years of assuming things and my kid brings me a margin full of doubts. Kohen teach you that too?"

"That one's mine," Thomas said. He turned the pad toward her and set the pen down between them on the table, the way you offer the next move to somebody.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
story:
Hudson was not nervous about the speech, which is why he had rewritten it four times and why his mother had finally told him to go outside and stop pacing a groove into the kitchen floor. He drove to the school parking lot because it was the one place nobody would look for him on graduation morning, the asphalt already shimmering with heat, the lines of empty stalls stretched out like staff paper with nothing written on them. He had the speech folded in his breast pocket. He had no intention of taking it out. He was only there to think.

Louis-Thomas found him anyway, because Louis-Thomas always found him, leaning his bike against the trunk of a car that belonged to some teacher who had left hours ago. "You look like a guy rehearsing," Louis-Thomas said, dropping onto the concrete barrier beside him.

"I'm not rehearsing. I'm sitting." Hudson had, in fact, been mouthing the third paragraph when Louis-Thomas rolled up. He had also practiced it in the shower, twice in the car, and once into the mirror of the boys' bathroom at the gas station, which he would deny under oath.

"It's a farewell speech," Louis-Thomas said. "That's literally what the word means. Vale dicere, Latin, to say farewell. That's the whole job. You say goodbye to people." He plucked a dandelion from a crack in the asphalt and began stripping it of seeds one by one. Marie-Pier had told him the same thing last week, and he'd said it back to Hudson as though he'd discovered it himself, but Hudson didn't know that, and it landed like news.

Hudson turned the phrase over. He had been trying to write something sagacious, something with the weight of an ending, a speech about futures and doors and journeys, and every draft had come out sounding like a poster in a dentist's office. He had assumed the problem was that he wasn't serious enough. Now it occurred to him that the problem might be the opposite: he was being too grand. Nobody in that gymnasium wanted the meaning of life from an eighteen-year-old in a rented gown. Maybe they just wanted to be told goodbye, honestly, by someone who had actually looked at them. He wasn't sure that version was in him either. Both ideas sat side by side in his head and refused to merge into anything he could commit to paper.

"It's corny, though," he said. "Saying goodbye is corny."

"Says the guy mouthing his speech in an empty parking lot."

"I wasn't mouthing anything."

Louis-Thomas let the last seed go and watched the wind take it toward the gym doors, where the custodian was propping them open for the chairs that would be dragged out at noon. "Look, you don't have to make it not corny. You just have to make it true. Corny and true can ride in the same car."

Hudson finally took the folded pages from his pocket. Four drafts, crossouts everywhere, the word "journey" struck through so hard the pen had torn the paper. Underneath, in the margin, he had scribbled names. Marie-Pier. The chemistry lab that had smelled like burnt hair for a week. The time the bus got stuck in the snow and Ms. Sánchez had led them all in singing until the driver laughed himself into a better mood. He had told himself the names were just notes, a substrate for the real speech, the important part. Reading them now, in the flat light of the lot, he suspected the names were the speech, and the rest had been decoration. He couldn't prove it. That was the part that kept snagging: he had two theories of what a speech owed people, the grand one and the small one, and no way to know which was right before he was already standing at the podium with three hundred people waiting.

He stood up, which surprised him, and read the margin aloud to Louis-Thomas, just the names, just the small things, his voice cracking once on Ms. Sánchez. When he finished, Louis-Thomas was quiet for a second, then nodded at the gym. "That one. Do that one."

"Even if it's corny?"

"Especially." Louis-Thomas swung his leg back over the bike. "What time do they lock this lot?"

Hudson looked at his watch, at the doors, at the dandelion stem lying in the dust. He folded the pages once more, along a new crease, so that the margin with the names sat on the outside.

"Ten," he said, and started walking toward the gym.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Kyle arrived at the coffee shop eleven minutes early, which he understood was its own kind of mistake, because now he had nothing to do but rearrange the sugar dispenser and watch the door. He had requisitioned the corner table by the window, the one with two chairs instead of the booth, because a booth felt like a commitment and two chairs could be pulled closer or pushed apart depending on how the next hour went. When Jayden came through the door shaking rain off her jacket, he stood so fast he knocked the sugar dispenser over and had to catch it with both hands, which was, he decided, the least cool thing he had done all year, and possibly the most honest.

"You got me a coffee?" she said. There was a cup waiting at her place, and she read the sleeve before sitting. "Oat milk. Okay, you listened."

"You mentioned it once. In September." He sat back down before his legs could do anything else embarrassing. Jayden was in his psychology class, which was where this whole thing had started, more or less, with a debate about whether personality could change that had gone on so long after the bell that Mr. Kaya had finally locked the classroom around them and said, "Either continue this outside my room or transfer to the debate team."

The first twenty minutes went well. They covered the rain, the coffee, the fact that Kyle's younger brother was irascible before breakfast and borderline feral after it, the fact that Jayden's mother had recently begun dating a man who referred to himself, unironically, as a hedonist. Then the well ran dry. Kyle could feel it happening, the silence stretching, each of them reaching for a topic and finding the shelf empty, and he thought about how his father described first dates as interviews where both applicants pretended not to be applying. He didn't want it to be that.

Jayden solved it first. "Okay," she said, turning her cup a quarter turn on the table. "This is going to sound like a stunt, but I read about this thing. This study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal as they went, and afterward those pairs ended up feeling closer than pairs who just made small talk."

"Thirty-six," Kyle said.

"Thirty-six. I looked it up again last night. I was going to save it for an emergency, but we're at the emergency, so." She pulled her phone out, then paused with her thumb over the screen. "Unless you think it's fake intimacy. I went back and forth on that for like an hour."

He thought about it honestly, which was a thing he was trying to make a habit of. On one side: a protocol, borrowed closeness, feelings manufactured in a lab and worn like a borrowed jacket. On the other side: what was small talk doing that was so authentic? Reciting his class schedule at her wasn't a purer path to knowing him. Maybe the questions were less like a shortcut and more like a door, and a door was only fake if you refused to walk through it. He also suspected he was rationalizing, because he wanted very much to walk through it, and he could hold both of those thoughts at once without either one winning. "I don't know if it's real," he said. "But I know the alternative is asking you about the weather again, and I'd rather find out."

She slid the phone across so he could see the screen. "You start. Alternate."

The first questions were almost too easy, and they laughed at how easy, which itself loosened something. Then the middle arrived, the questions about embarrassment and gratitude and the last time she had cried in front of another person, and Kyle heard himself telling her about his grandfather's funeral, which he had not told anyone at school about, and watched her not look away. When her turn came she talked about moving schools in eighth grade and deciding, deliberately, to become a different person, and then about the strangeness of that person now fitting better than the original, and Kyle understood that she had just handed him something that could not be handed back.

By the twenties they had both scooted their chairs in without either of them announcing it. He noticed, when she got cold, that she kept her hands around the cup instead of asking for anything, so he got up and requisitioned the last blueberry muffin from the case and set it between them, and she tore off half without ceremony, which he took as a good sign.

Somewhere around question thirty-two, she said, "Okay, this one I actually want to skip. It's the death one." Then she was quiet for a second, and Kyle watched her decide. "No. I'll do it. My grandpa, last spring. I was the one who found out first and had to tell my mom." She said it flatly, the way you carry something heavy with a straight back, and Kyle didn't reach for her hand, though he thought about it, because they had known each other for a year and this for forty minutes, and both of those facts were true and they pulled in opposite directions.

When they finished, neither of them said anything about feeling closer, which Kyle was grateful for, because saying it would have flattened it. He still didn't know whether the study proved something about people or something about surveys, and he told her so, and she said, "That's fine, we don't have to know everything," and turned her cup another quarter turn.

Outside the window the rain had thinned to something almost invisible, and her bus would come eventually, and there were still four questions on the screen they had skipped in their hurry to talk around them. She looked at the phone, then at him, and pulled her chair another inch closer.

"Question thirty-four," she said. "Your turn to answer first."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: When a candidate's lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll cannot say with confidence who is ahead, but that does not mean the race is exactly tied.
story:
The group chat had been named "Costa's Revenge" after the AP Stats teacher who had once told them, on the last day of junior year, that they would use his class whether they liked it or not. Now, three days before the local election, the chat was moving faster than Brooklyn had ever seen it. Guillaume had posted a screenshot of a poll, then another poll, then a third, each with a different number, and Mathias had responded with a single word: rigged. Brooklyn sat on her bedroom floor with her laptop open, her chemistry notes beside her, the word allotrope half-copied into a flashcard, and watched the argument build.

"48 to 46," Guillaume typed. "Ramirez by two. It's over."

"It's a tie," Mathias typed back. "Read the article. It says statistical tie. That means nobody's ahead."

"That's not what that means."

"It literally says tie."

Brooklyn could see where this was going, and it was going nowhere. She typed "wait" three times, watched it sit unanswered between their messages, then called Guillaume instead. He picked up on the second ring; she could hear the campaign office behind him, phones, a printer, someone laughing near the window. He was volunteering there after school, transcribing call sheets into the voter database, and Mathias had started showing up too, mostly to argue.

"Put me on speaker," she said. "I want Mathias to hear this."

"You're on speaker," Guillaume said. "He's eating the volunteer pretzels."

"Those are for everyone," Mathias said, mouth full.

"Okay," Brooklyn said. "Mathias. The poll is 48 to 46. What's the margin of error?"

"Four," he said. "Four percent, something like that."

"And what's the lead?"

"Two."

"So think about what the margin of error is for. It's not a wall around a tie. It's how much the numbers could be off." She heard herself slow down, because this part mattered and she didn't want to get it wrong in front of both of them. "When a candidate's lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll can't say with confidence who's ahead. But that doesn't mean the race is exactly tied. That's it. That's the whole thing."

There was a silence on the line except for the office noise, the printer finishing a page. Then Mathias said, "So it's a tie."

"No," Brooklyn said. "You're not listening. It's a tie the way a coin that might be weighted is a tie. We don't know. The poll can't tell us. That's different from the poll telling us it's even."

"Same thing," Mathias said, but his voice had lost its edge, the way it did in class when he was turning an idea over rather than defending it. "So the article's lying."

"The article's lazy," Guillaume said. "It's easier to print 'statistical tie' than to print 'we have no idea.'"

Brooklyn looked at her flashcard, allotrope, a different physical form of the same element, graphite and diamond, the same thing arranged differently, and thought about how "tied" and "unknown" were like that. Same words on the page, different structure underneath. She didn't say it out loud. "Here's my actual question," she said instead. "Guillaume, you're in that office. What are they doing about it?"

There was a pause, and in the pause she heard him cover the phone, not well, a muffled exchange she couldn't make out, then his voice again, closer, meant only for her and Mathias. "They think we're going to lose," he said. "The field director said the internal numbers look worse than the public ones. But I'm not supposed to repeat that."

"Then why did you?" Mathias asked.

"Because you two are the only people I know who'll understand what it does and doesn't mean."

Brooklyn closed her laptop halfway, the screen tilting the kitchen light across her knees. She understood what he was doing. The internal numbers were another poll, another estimate with its own margin, its own uncertainty, and he was handing them a fact that could be read as doom or as noise. Mathias would call it over. Guillaume had already called it over. The office was deciding, tonight, whether to spend its last weekend on the district where that 48 to 46 had been measured, or to abandon it for safer ground.

"So what do we do," Mathias said. It wasn't really a question to her; it was a question into the room.

"We don't treat it as a tie," Brooklyn said. "We also don't treat it as a win. It's not exactly tied and it's not exactly a lead. It's just a small thing we can't see clearly yet." She heard how little that sounded like an answer, and she let it stand anyway, because the other options were lies. "If I were them, I'd go. But I can't tell you why beyond that it feels closer to true."

"Ramirez is at 48," Guillaume said slowly, as if reading it off something. "In the internal one too. She's at 48 and she was at 48 last week. The other number moved."

Brooklyn sat up. "Which one moved?"

"Hold on." The phone rustled; she heard him cross the office, the phones, the laughter now behind him, a door. Then he came back on, quiet. "The other guy's at 49."

In the chat, the poll screenshot still sat at the top of the thread, 48 to 46, statistical tie, and neither of them typed anything for a long moment. Mathias broke it, finally, with three words.

"Guys. Pretzels?"

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
Christopher counted the bills twice at the kitchen table before he left, because the number mattered. Six hundred and forty dollars, saved from two summers of bagging groceries, and today it was going into an account whose sole purpose was a car. At the bank he stood in the line that moved slowest, holding the deposit slip the way other people held winning tickets. The teller, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, stamped his copy and said, "You're building something," and he said, "Trying to," which felt closer to the truth.

The car was Gwen's mother's, a gray sedan with a coffee stain shaped like Portugal on the passenger seat, and Gwen rode along because her mother insisted someone licensed be in the car, though Gwen mostly provided commentary. Christopher was eighteen days from his road test, and he could not parallel park. He had requisitioned traffic cones from the school custodian by promising to return them unbattered, and he had set them up along the curb behind the bank, where the parking lot was empty on Sundays. The bank loomed over the practice like a judge.

"You're eight feet out," Gwen said from the curb, arms crossed. "The test guy wants you within a foot of the curb, and you have to do it in three moves or it's automatic points."

"I know the specs." He knew the specs the way he knew the quadratic formula, abstractly, in a way that evaporated under observation. He pulled forward, reversed with his hand on the passenger headrest, turned the wheel, and heard the soft thud of a cone going under the tire. Gwen retrieved it without comment, which was worse than vitriolic commentary would have been. He tried again. The car slid in crooked, angled like something caught mid-argument.

"You have to commit," Gwen said. "You keep stopping halfway."

On the fourth attempt he committed, swung the wheel hard, and the sedan settled against the curb with the front tire an inch away. He sat with his hands still on the wheel, breathing. Gwen came and crouched by the door. "Six inches," she said. "But you took five moves."

They drove out to the highway after that, because the test route included a merge and Christopher had never merged above forty. Gwen had a laminated page from the driver's manual in the door pocket, its corners soft from handling. Construction narrowed the road from two lanes to one three miles ahead, and a sign ordered traffic to move left, and the left lane slowed to a crawl. Christopher signalled immediately and nudged toward the gap a station wagon reluctantly gave him.

"Actually, don't," Gwen said. "Stay in this lane."

"The sign says merge left."

"I know, but Isaac says you're supposed to use both lanes all the way to the end. It's called the zipper merge. Minnesota's Department of Transportation says using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent."

Christopher looked in the mirror. The right lane ahead was empty, arrow-straight, and using it felt like line-cutting, like the thing his mother called rudeness and Mr. Kaur, his economics teacher, would have called an individual strategy that fails if everybody distrusts it. But the left lane was not moving, and the right lane was the road saying what roads are for. He signalled off, rolled forward alone, and reached the cones where a worker in an orange vest waved him alternately with a car from the left. One car, then him. The sedan ahead of him in the left lane, a truck with a gun rack, let him in with a small, surprised gap, and no one honked.

"So it works," Christopher said, "if everyone agrees to take turns."

"If everyone takes turns," Gwen said, which was not the same thing, and she was looking at the truck's mirror, where the driver was watching them.

They did the merge twice more and returned to the cones behind the bank as the sun dropped. On his last parallel attempt, the car slid in on the first try, four moves, and when he looked at Gwen she held up a hand, fingers spread, then folded her thumb. Nine inches. He would still be practicing Thursday, and the examiner would still be a stranger with a clipboard, and somewhere ahead of him was every merge he would ever make alone, in traffic that had never read a study and did not intend to. He put the car in park between the cones and left it there, engine ticking, exactly where it belonged.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The power rule says the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus 1, so the derivative of x cubed is 3x squared.
story:
Oliver had agreed to meet Konnor at the tutoring centre on a Tuesday he would rather have spent anywhere else, because Konnor had texted him a photo of a calculus worksheet captioned "check this for me, you're the math guy now," and because Oliver, deep down, wanted to be the math guy. He arrived to find Konnor already installed at the corner table with a large iced coffee that was, by law of the centre's posted ordinance, not permitted past the doorway, and Konnor was drinking it anyway with the calm of someone who had read the sign and decided it applied to other people.

"So I did the whole page," Konnor said, sliding the worksheet across. "Took me like an hour. Fairly proud of it, honestly."

Oliver looked down at the paper. The problem asked for the derivative of x to the power n, and Konnor had written, in surprisingly neat handwriting, that it came out to n times x to the power n. Below that, for the derivative of x cubed, he had written 3x cubed. Oliver read it twice, then a third time, because he wanted to be sure before he said anything. He had only learned this himself two weeks ago, at this same table, on a night when the rain on the windows had seemed to presage a long and fruitless evening, and the discovery had been the one bright thing in it.

"Your coefficients are right," Oliver said, which was true, and which he said first because he had learned from his mother that you lead with the good news. "You brought the power down in front. Every single problem."

"Right. Power rule. I remembered the bringing-down part."

"But you left the power where it was. You have to lower it by one. The derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power n minus one. So for x cubed..."

Konnor stared at his own paper as though it had betrayed him personally. "So it's 3x squared. Not 3x cubed."

"3x squared."

"For the whole page? Every answer?"

"Every answer," Oliver said, and he tried to say it gently, but a laugh escaped anyway, and Konnor laughed too, the defeated laugh of a man who has just discovered that his one hour of effort produced a page of answers that were wrong in exactly the same way, which Konnor declared was at least "consistent, like a theme."

Evelyne, who tutored the middle-schoolers on Thursdays and had drifted over on the pretense of borrowing a stapler, looked at the worksheet over Konnor's shoulder. "You forgot to lower the power," she said. "That's endemic with this one. Everyone forgets. I forgot. My whole class forgot."

"My whole page forgot," Konnor said.

Ms. Van Dijk, who ran the centre and had a talent for appearing at the exact moment something was being worked out, did not rescue anyone. She set a fresh worksheet on the table, one with a single problem on it, a polynomial with a maximum to locate, and said only, "When you've fixed the first page, try this," and walked away to argue gently with a seventh grader about the location of the stapler.

The new problem was harder than anything Konnor's teacher had assigned. Oliver could feel the shape of the method, how the derivative would go to zero somewhere and that somewhere would be the top of the curve, but the details kept sliding. He and Konnor worked it side by side, Konnor lowering powers with exaggerated care, announcing "lowered" each time like a man landing a plane, while Oliver multiplied terms on a scrap paper that was rapidly running out of scrap. Twice he got one sign wrong and Konnor caught it, which seemed to restore Konnor's faith in the universe. Twice Oliver caught Konnor forgetting, again, to lower the power, and Konnor said "lowered, lowered" and fixed it.

The answer they finally reached was a maximum at x equals 2, and Oliver was eighty percent sure it was right, which he said out loud, because he had decided somewhere in the last hour that pretending to certainty was its own kind of forgetting. Ms. Van Dijk came back, looked at the page, looked at the two of them, and raised an eyebrow that could have meant correct or could have meant almost, and offered nothing further, which Oliver chose to find encouraging.

"Same time next week?" Konnor said, capping his illegal iced coffee. "I'll bring contraband for you too."

Oliver gathered the scrap paper, both worksheets, the pencil he had chewed into a state Konnor described as "endangered." Outside, the streetlights were coming on.

"Bring the one with the staples," he said. "Evelyne kept the stapler."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
Alicia stood in Campbell's kitchen holding a cup of punch she didn't want, watching Waylon try to juggle three limes at the birthday party. He dropped them twice, and the second time he laughed and called himself a klutz, and everyone laughed with him, and something in her chest went tight. Two days before, at practice, she had told him, in front of the whole relay squad, that he always ruined the handoffs. She had been trying to be honest. It had come out like a knife, and he hadn't spoken to her since except in flat one-word answers.

Mr. Whitehead, who lived next door to Campbell and had drifted over for cake, was telling a story near the counter about his years teaching chemistry. "I had a student once," he said, "who insisted enthalpy was just a word I'd invented to ruin her weekend." Alicia smiled at that without meaning to, because the same student's older sister had cajoled her into joining the track team in the first place, back in ninth grade, with promises of glory and free orange slices.

She had spent last night writing Waylon a message, and she still had it saved on her phone, unsent. She ducked into the hallway to reread it under the coat rack. "I was thinking about what happened at practice," it said. "I read something tonight. This psychologist, John Gottman, says a complaint is different from criticism. A complaint goes at a specific thing you did, like 'you missed practice twice.' Criticism goes at who you are, like 'you always mess up.' I gave you the second one dressed up as the first. What I actually wanted to say was that when you're at practice, the handoffs are clean, and when you miss them, I want to know what's going on so we can fix it together. You don't have to answer this. Happy birthday to Campbell, anyway."

When she looked up, Campbell was standing at the end of the hall with two paper plates of cake, holding one out. "You're hiding," Campbell said. "At my own party. That's basically a crime." Alicia took the plate. Campbell nodded at the phone still lit in her hand. "Still haven't sent it?" "How'd you know?" "Because you've typed and deleted the same thing four times since Tuesday. I can hear your thumbs from across the room."

In the living room someone had put on music, and Waylon was sitting on the arm of the couch, working through his own slice of cake in careful bites. Alicia stood in the doorway with her plate and her unsent message, and she made a small decision that felt enormous: she pressed send. Then she walked over and sat on the floor near his feet, because the couch was full, and because sitting on the floor was a way of saying she wasn't going to loom over him.

His phone buzzed in his pocket. He didn't check it. He said, "Good cake," to no one in particular, and she said, "The frosting's the best part," and for a minute they were two people talking about cake, which was its own kind of mercy. Then he pulled out his phone, glanced at it, and went still.

"You could've just said that at practice," he said finally, not looking up. "The part about the handoffs being clean when I'm there." "I know," Alicia said. "I turned a complaint into a criticism and aimed it at you in front of everyone. The specific thing was you missing Tuesday and Thursday. The thing I actually said was 'you always ruin it,' which isn't even true, and it wasn't about the handoffs at all. It was about me being scared of losing." Waylon set his plate down. "It was about my shift at the restaurant," he said. "They changed my schedule and I couldn't get out of it. I was going to tell the coach." "Then tell me too," she said. "Next time. Even if it's just a text." He was quiet, and she let the quiet sit there instead of rushing to fill it, which was another thing she was learning, slowly, the way she was learning everything.

Campbell flopped onto the couch arm beside Waylon and said, "If you two are going to be facetious and reconciled, you have to do it in the kitchen, where the rest of us can watch." Waylon stood and offered Alicia a hand up from the floor, and she took it, and she still didn't know whether the relay squad would make sectionals, or whether one honest text could outweigh a public wound. But he was walking toward the kitchen with her, and on the counter the last two slices of cake sat side by side, waiting.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The video arrived on Alice's phone during fourth period, forwarded by Gia with a row of exclamation marks: a warehouse on fire, firefighters dwarfed by the smoke, and a caption claiming it was the food processing plant outside town, burning this morning. By lunch, half the school had seen it. Moses had already sent it to his mother, who worked second shift at a distribution center two streets from the plant, and she had left her shift early to drive past and make sure everyone had gotten out.

Alice wanted to share it too. She had a cousin who worked receiving, and the thought of being the one to warn her first made her thumb hover over the forward arrow. But something about the clip bothered her, a flatness she couldn't name, and instead she typed "reverse image search video" into the browser on her phone, tucked behind her binder in study hall. The results were useless at first. She dragged the video file into the image search box and the engine refused it, again and again, as though she were trying to mail a letter in a parcel box. Then, lower on the page, a fact-checking site mentioned in passing that their researchers search screenshots of key frames. So that was the trick: a video could not go in, but a picture pulled out of it could.

She paused the clip where the smoke was thickest, took a screenshot, trimmed the black bars off the edges with the crop tool, and fed that image into the search. The matches loaded slowly on the school's wifi. When they came, they came all at once: the same warehouse, the same crooked ladder of flame, dated four years ago and an ocean away, in a story about a chemical fire no one in this town had ever heard of. She scrolled further and found it again, recycled last year with a different false caption, then again the year before that. The fire was real; it had simply never happened here.

She found Gia in the gymnasium lobby and held out the phone. "Look at the dates." Gia squinted at the screen, then at Alice, then back at the screen.

"So I sent a lie to two hundred people."

"You sent what you thought was news," Alice said, and immediately heard how hollow the comfort was.

Ms. Bondarenko, who supervised study hall and had drifted over at the commotion, glanced at the screens without reaching for her glasses. "That trick," she said, "with the screenshot. Who taught you that?" Alice shrugged and said nobody, and Ms. Bondarenko nodded once and walked on, which somehow felt like more of an award than anything the school gave out at assemblies.

The hard part came after. Moses's mother had already been home for an hour by the time he corrected the post, and she had called three coworkers in a panic, and one of them had a diabetic son she couldn't reach until evening. Moses didn't blame Alice, exactly. He said it was Gia's forward, and the stranger who made the video, and the way the whole school seemed to inculcate a kind of reflex in them all, share first, verify never, as if speed were its own virtue. He said it with a trenchant little laugh that Alice suspected he'd practiced, and she couldn't argue, because she had almost done the same thing. Her thumb had been on the arrow. The only difference between her and Gia was twenty minutes and a screenshot.

In English the next week they were doing persuasive essays, and the teacher kept asking "what is the purpose of this paragraph," "what is the purpose of this statistic," purpose, purpose, until Alice wrote in the margin of her notes that bad information seemed to have a teleology of its own: designed to be forwarded, engineered to arrive exactly when caring would make you careless. She wasn't sure that was grammatically what teleology meant, and she looked it up, and it was close enough, though she decided not to put the word in the final draft. Some words explained more than the thing they explained.

She corrected her cousin too, an hour late, with the screenshot and the link and a paragraph she deleted down to two sentences. Her cousin replied with a thumbs up and "good looking out," and then, separately: "weird that I believed it instantly." Alice stared at that message for a long time, because she had no answer. She still didn't know why the video had snagged on her and not on anyone else, whether it was suspicion or luck or some coldness in her that kept her from trusting a fire when she saw one. Gia, meanwhile, had started checking everything, including things that were true, and had gone quiet in a way Alice couldn't tell was guilt or a new kind of careful.

On Friday a new clip started circulating, a flood in a parking lot that was allegedly last night, three towns over. Alice watched it once, set her phone face down on the lunch table, and pulled up the crop tool. Gia slid into the seat across from her without a word and turned her own phone around, already showing the search results.

"It's from 2019," Gia said. "Louisiana."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
The line at the church on Ashwood Avenue went out the door and bent around the bicycle rack, and Autumn joined it with her passport in one hand and her voter card in the other, except she didn't have a voter card, and that was the problem. She had turned eighteen in March. Her mother had said something about a card coming in the mail weeks ago, and Autumn had nodded the way she nodded at most things in the spring, and now it was election day and there was no card on the fridge, no card anywhere.

"Move up," said the man behind her, querulous, gesturing at the gap she'd left. She stepped forward. Ahead of her, Ayaan from her economics class stood in his coat, thumbs moving over his phone.

"You're here too," he said, not really looking up. "You registered, right?"

"I got the thing in the mail," she said, and then, because lying to Ayaan felt heavier than the lie was worth, "I think I did. My mom said something about a card."

"My dad's whole speech this morning," Ayaan said. "If you don't vote you can't complain. Like complaining is the reward. Voting is just buying a license to be miserable in public."

"That's not the alternative, though." The line moved. Through the open doors she could smell coffee and floor wax, and somewhere a photocopier grinding. "The alternative to his speech isn't nihilism. You can care and still think one ballot doesn't move much."

"One ballot doesn't," Ayaan said. "That's arithmetic, not nihilism."

At the check-in table, a woman with a clipboard asked for his card, scanned it, and he went through the second doors without saying goodbye. Then it was Autumn's turn. The woman asked her name, typed it, frowned at her screen, typed again.

"There's no one by that name at this poll," she said. "Are you sure you're registered?"

The floor wax smell got sharper, or Autumn noticed it more. "I'm eighteen. Since March. I thought it was automatic."

"It's not," the woman said, not unkindly. Then, over her shoulder, "Sir, can you take this one?"

Mr. Nolan, who had taught her Grade 11 history and now apparently worked these elections in a grey polo, came around the table. He raised his eyebrows at her, and for a second she thought he was going to start on one of his lectures, the ones that could circumscribe an entire lunch period. He didn't. "Show her," was all he said to the woman.

The woman pulled a form from a folder. "You can register right here, today," she said. "At your assigned polling place, on election day. Bring ID with your address." She slid the form and a pen across the table.

"That's allowed?" Autumn asked. "On the day itself?"

"That's the rule."

She wrote her name and her address in handwriting that came out smaller than she'd intended, and the woman checked her passport, checked a utility bill her mother had made her take that morning like it was a permission slip, and stapled something, and Mr. Nolan initialed a corner without ceremony. Then he pointed her toward the second doors and went back to the table, and that was it. No speech. She had expected to feel something marked, a hinge swinging, and instead a man with a clipboard said "Booth twelve" and she walked over worn carpet to a cardboard stand with a pencil on a string.

Behind the little screen, the ballot was smaller than she'd imagined. The names of the candidates ran down the left side in alphabetical order, and the marks of her whole education, the debates in Mr. Nolan's class, the arguments with Ayaan about whether principles mattered if nothing changed, all of it narrowed to one pencil and a few centimetres of paper. She thought about her mother mailing something, or not mailing it, and about how she'd almost walked home instead of getting in line, because being turned away would have been easier to explain to herself than standing there exposed as careless.

She marked an X. It was crooked. She folded the ballot along the crease and carried it to the box, where a poll worker held out a hand. Gaelle, who had been two rows behind her in line, appeared at her elbow with her own folded ballot.

"Booth fourteen's pencil is broken," Gaelle said. "You vote yet?"

"Just now." Autumn slid her ballot into the slot and heard it land, a soft paper sound among all the others.

"Took you long enough at that table. They gave you trouble?"

"They let me register there. Today. I didn't know you could." Outside, the light had gone thin and gold on the parked cars, and Ayaan was leaning on the bicycle rack waiting for someone, maybe them. Gaelle dropped her ballot in, and Autumn said, "Come on, he owes us an argument about arithmetic."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
Jordan had been eighteen for exactly six days, which he kept repeating to himself like a password he was afraid to forget. He'd arranged to meet Catherine at the coffee shop on Grange Street because it was halfway between his apartment and the polling station set up in the gym of the old elementary school, and because he suspected that if he went alone he would stand outside the gym for ten minutes doing nothing and then go home.

"You look like a man about to have a minor medical procedure," Catherine said when she arrived. She put her bag on the chair between them and studied the chalkboard menu as though it were a document requiring her signature.

"I've never done it before," Jordan said. "That's all. Everyone acts like it's nothing, and then you get in there and it's apparently a whole system."

"Let me guess. You watched a video about it at two in the morning."

"Three videos," he said, and was embarrassed by how pleased he sounded. "There's a thing I can't stop thinking about, though. Nobody in the world is allowed to see how you mark it. There's a screen, a folded piece of paper, a box with a slot. And the video said the whole arrangement has a name, the Australian ballot, because the Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856." He hadn't meant to verbalize all of that; it came out in the tone of someone reciting a spell, and he regretted it.

Catherine ordered a filter coffee and he ordered the same, mostly to have something to do with his hands. She said, "So Australia invented privacy."

"That's facetious," Jordan said. "But also, kind of, yes. Before that, people could watch you vote. Out loud, in front of everyone. Your landlord, your boss, your uncle."

"Your uncle," she repeated, as though that were the decisive horror. She stirred a sugar in without drinking. "My mother says when she voted in her first election here, her father told her which name to pick, and she picked a different one, and never told him. She says it's the bravest thing she's ever done, and she once drove a delivery truck through a hailstorm."

Jordan turned his cup a quarter turn on its saucer. His own father had opinions the way other men had tattoos, permanent and on display, and Jordan had spent the last six days constructing a mental genealogy of those opinions: which ones he'd inherited, which ones he'd absorbed by proximity, and which, if any, he'd actually built himself. The trouble was that the three categories kept borrowing from each other. He could not always tell which thoughts were his.

"Here's what I keep going back and forth on," he said. "Part of me thinks secrecy is for cowards. If you believe something, say it with your face attached. Stand behind it. The other part thinks the secret ballot is the only thing that makes a vote actually yours, and that saying it out loud just makes it a performance for whoever's standing nearest." He heard how earnest it sounded, and Catherine let it sit for a moment, which was either generosity or punishment.

"My grandmother would tell you both things are true," she said. "She liked holding two ideas until they complained."

The line for the polling station ran along the gymnasium wall and out through the double doors into the cold. An older woman ahead of them kept turning around as though checking for someone she'd left at home, and a man with a clipboard was being told, gently and repeatedly, that he had to stay behind a line painted on the floor. When Jordan gave his name, the officer with the list found it, and there was a small ceremony to it, a pencil line, a folded paper, a booth with a little shelf. Inside, he stood for longer than he'd planned. He thought about Tasmania and Victoria, colonies on the far side of the world, arranging all this a hundred and seventy years ago so that some teenager in a gymnasium could stand alone with a pencil and no uncle in sight.

He marked the paper, folded it along its existing creases, and fed it into the box. Outside, Catherine was waiting with both coffees, having voted ahead of him.

"So," she said. "Are you going to tell me?"

"Tell you what?"

"How you voted."

Jordan wrapped his hands around his cup and looked at the gym doors, at the line still stretching out of them, at the man with the clipboard being escorted, still gently, toward the parking lot. "Ask my uncle," he said, and walked toward the car.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Georges Lefebvre's 1939 book, translated as The Coming of the French Revolution, described 1789 as four revolutions: aristocratic, bourgeois, urban popular and peasant.
story:
The library had given Andrew the far table by the microfilm machines, the one nobody used anymore, and he had spread his sources across it like a man trying to collate a life's worth of mail. Three books on the French Revolution, a photocopy of a journal article with the margins eaten by the copier, and a page of notes that dissolved into a doodle of a guillotine halfway down. His assignment sheet, folded twice, said: "How have historians' views of the Revolution changed since 1800? Take a position. Six pages." He had two and a half, and the position they took was roughly that historians disagreed, which his teacher, Mr. Chen, had already crossed out in red on his outline.

Sandra found him there at four, dropped her bag on a chair, and peered at the guillotine. "That's facetious," she said, tapping it. "You can't put that in an essay about the Terror."

"I wasn't going to put it in the essay. It's a thinking drawing."

"You think with severed heads?"

He turned his notebook over. She was applying to art schools and had opinions about his handwriting, his taste in pens, and once, memorably, his haircut, delivered as though all three were urgent matters of public record. Today she had a reason to be there, a bibliography of her own due Monday, and she settled across from him with a laptop covered in stickers and a silence that was, for Sandra, uncharacteristic. He noticed she kept glancing at his books.

"You can take one," he said finally. "I'm not using them all."

"I'm not here for your books." She typed for a while. Then: "Elisabeth said you got into the summer program. The history one at the university."

He hadn't told anyone except his mother, and his mother had asked whether it paid. "Mr. Chen nominated me. It's just six weeks."

"That's huge, Andrew." She said it flatly, still typing, and he understood that something had been decided between them without him being consulted, as things often were. She had applied to the same program. He knew because he had seen her name on the list in Mr. Chen's classroom, two lines above his own, and he had thought about that list every day since without once saying so.

He pulled the nearest book back toward him so he would have somewhere to look. It was a fat paperback, The Coming of the French Revolution, by Georges Lefebvre, and he had been avoiding it because the introduction was dense and French names tended to shed letters when he wasn't watching. He read a page, then another, and then something on page three made him stop and go back. Lefebvre, writing in 1939, hadn't treated 1789 as one event at all. He described it as four revolutions happening at once: an aristocratic revolution, a bourgeois revolution, an urban popular revolution, and a peasant revolution.

"Four revolutions," he said out loud, forgetting where he was.

Sandra looked up. "In one year?"

"In one summer, basically. The nobles rebelled first, then the middle class, then the townspeople, then the peasants, all overlapping, all wanting different things." He was already writing, fast, the doodle buried under arrows. His essay's problem had been that historians kept describing the same event in opposite ways, bourgeois triumph or popular catastrophe, and he had been trying to pick a lane. But if 1789 itself was several revolutions braided together, then the historians weren't exactly contradicting each other. They were looking at different strands.

He drafted a paragraph right there at the table, pen skipping, about how the Marxists who followed Lefebvre and the revisionists who tore him apart decades later might partly be describing different revolutions within the Revolution. It was the first thing he'd written in two weeks that felt like a claim instead of a hedge. He didn't know yet whether it would survive Monday. Probably some of it was too neat. Probably Mr. Chen would find the seams. But that, Andrew thought, was the whole discipline, wasn't it, making the argument you could actually defend and admitting the shape of what you couldn't.

Sandra closed her laptop. "I didn't get in, if you're wondering. She told me Thursday." She said it lightly, the way she said everything, so that he could take it either as a wound or as nothing, at his own risk. "Elisabeth thinks I should appeal, but Elisabeth is an aesthete, she thinks everything is a dramatic gesture." She stood, hooked her bag over her shoulder. "Read me your paragraph. The four revolutions one."

He read it. The library hummed around them, the microfilm machines blank and patient, someone's cart squeaking past the periodicals. When he finished she stood there a moment with her hand on the chair back.

"It's good," she said. "It's actually good." Then she pushed the chair in, all the way, careful, the way you would at someone else's house, and walked out through the security gates without looking back.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: French economist Frédéric Bastiat's 1850 essay 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' argued that good economics must count the effects nobody sees.
story:
Caleb had been at the register long enough to know that the fourth cup of the afternoon always went to the man in the gray windbreaker, who always paid in exact change, and that the fifth was usually Umar's, because Umar's shift at the bookstore across the mall ended at three and he liked to loiter.

"Still hiring?" Umar asked, dropping his backpack onto the counter where the napkins were supposed to be.

"Two shifts a week. Maybe three." Caleb rang him up for a small drip, which Umar never drank; he bought it the way you buy a ticket, for the right to stand there and talk.

Umar pulled a folded schedule from his pocket. "Economics with Friedman. She teaches it like it's a religion." He flattened the paper on the counter, and Caleb leaned over the pastry case to read it. Halfway down the list of readings, under a cluster of textbook chapters, sat a title: "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen," an essay by Frédéric Bastiat, 1850.

"What does that even mean?"

"It means the French guy was mad about a broken window," Umar said, and then the espresso machine shrieked and he had to wait, and by the time it stopped he'd lost the thread. "I didn't do the reading. Ask her, she loves that stuff."

Caleb did not ask her, because Ms. Friedman was the sort of teacher whose attention felt like a searchlight, and Caleb was eighteen and had perfected the art of being unremarkable. But he thought about the title while he wiped down the milk steamer. That which is seen. The obvious thing. His mother, when she'd taken the second job, had said it was only for a year, and that had been two years ago, and what she'd given up for it was never anything you could point to. It was just the thing that didn't happen.

Jaylen came in at four for his own coffee, which he also didn't finish, and the three of them occupied the window booth in a loose conspiracy of stalling. Jaylen was telling them about the internship his father had arranged, something at a logistics firm with a name like a lawnmower brand. "Paid," he kept saying. "Forty hours, all summer, paid."

"And you're taking it?"

"I'd be an idiot not to." Jaylen said it cheerfully, the way people say things they haven't examined. He valorized the offer precisely because his father had arranged it, Caleb thought, which was maybe unkind, and probably true.

"I don't know," Caleb said. "I turned down the extra shifts here for July. Coach wanted me at summer league."

Jaylen looked at him with genuine, uncomplicated pity. "You're picking basketball over money."

"No," Caleb said, and then stopped, because he didn't have the end of the sentence. He picked up his cup, which was empty, and put it down again.

Umar, who had been scrolling his phone, looked up. "Bastiat," he said. "I found a summary. It's an 1850 essay, French economist, and he says good economics has to count the effects nobody sees." He read it off the screen flatly, like a weather report. "That's the whole thing, apparently. Everybody counts the broken window and the glazier's new business. Nobody counts what the money would have bought if the window hadn't broken."

The manager poked her head out of the back and Caleb went to restock cups, and while he did it he assembled the idea carefully, the way you stack paper.
