Jaylen's internship was the seen thing: forty hours, a paycheck, a line on a résumé. The unseen thing was whatever Jaylen would otherwise have done with the summer, and Jaylen himself had no idea what that was, which was the problem. You couldn't grieve a thing you'd never pictured. His mother's second job, his own skipped shifts, the summer league games he'd miss if he took the manager's offer of more hours, which she had made again that morning, twice, in a tone of nascent impatience. Every choice was a broken window in reverse. You got the window, and the glass you didn't get was invisible, and people like Jaylen's father walked around pointing only at windows.

He also suspected, stacking cups with more force than the cups required, that this could become a convenient philosophy. A way to claim every road not taken as a loss, to treat your imaginary summers as real ones. There was a kid at school who talked like that, who'd valorized his own rejections into a portfolio of parallel lives, and Caleb found the mendacity of it boring, the way it made every decision heroic. The unseen effects were real, probably. They were also uncountable, exactly as advertised, and something you couldn't count could be anything, including nothing.

At closing he took out the trash and found Ms. Friedman in the parking lot, loading paper bags into a hatchback. She nodded at his apron. "So you're the one Umar trails back here. He says you argued with Jaylen about opportunity cost for twenty minutes."

"I didn't know it had a name."

"It has a name, a Frenchman, and a body count." She shut the hatch. "Bastiat's essay is on the syllabus. 1850. 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen.'" She said it as if reciting a menu. "Read it before you decide I'm worth arguing with."

Inside, the manager asked him one more time about July, and this time she put a number on it, an actual figure per week, and Caleb stood at the counter with the drawer open in front of him, counting the day's money into neat stacks, each bill he set down making a small definite sound.

"Can I have until Friday?"

She said Friday. Behind her, through the window, the mall's lamps were coming on across the lot, and somewhere past them was the gym, and past the gym was everything else. He put the last stack down and squared it with his thumb.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera; they remarried the following year.
story:
Jessica had chosen the art history elective at camp mostly to fill the afternoon slot between canoeing and dinner, and now she sat on the floor of the lodge with a poster of The Two Fridas propped against the fireplace, trying to decide which of the two women she was supposed to believe. Mr. Nkosi had given them a handout on formal analysis, colour and composition and symbolism, and told them only that the painting would tell them everything they needed if they looked long enough. He refused, maddeningly, to tell them anything else.

"The one on the left is colder," Lilianne said, lying on her stomach with her chin in her hands. "All that white, and the grey sky. She looks like a ghost of the other one."

"Her dress is European," Bree said. She had the handout folded into a small square, which she opened and flattened whenever she wanted to sound official. "The right one is in the traditional dress. So it's two selves. Like, two countries, two histories."

Jessica wrote both observations down. Then she wrote, in the margin, the thing she actually thought: the left Frida has just cut the vein, and her blood is the only warm thing in her half of the canvas, a thin red line crossing the white dress. The heart she holds is whole but emptying. The right Frida holds a small portrait of someone, a man, and the vein connecting the two women runs from that portrait. Whoever the man was, the painting seemed to argue, the left Frida was losing him, and the right Frida still held him, and both of those things were true at once.

The lodge got loud as the evening session ended, and the three of them were the last at the poster. Mr. Nkosi came over and asked each of them for a thesis, one sentence, defensible from the canvas alone. Lilianne said the painting was about loneliness. Bree said it was about dual identity, colonized and colonizer, and Jessica could tell from Mr. Nkosi's small nod that this was the answer he had been fishing for all week. When it was her turn, Jessica said the painting was about a wound that had already been inflicted, not one that was coming; the blood was already on the dress, the sky already grey, so the image recorded a past event rather than portending one. It was, she said, like a deposition, a sworn statement of what had happened to the body, with the right Frida as the witness holding the evidence.

Mr. Nkosi raised one finger and went to the supply cupboard, where he kept a shoebox of postcards from a museum he'd visited years ago. He shuffled through them, didn't find what he wanted, and instead wrote something on a scrap of paper and handed it to Jessica without comment. It was the gallery label text, copied out. She read it twice. Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera. They remarried the following year.

"Divorced," Bree said, reading over her shoulder. "So the man in the little portrait, the one the vein comes from."

"He's the one she just lost," Jessica said slowly. "That's why the left one's bleeding. It's not symbolic blood, it's divorce blood. It happened that year, that exact year." She looked back at the poster and the painting rearranged itself in her head, the way a sentence does when you learn it was written on a particular day. The lugubrious sky, which she had been calling symbolic all week, now looked more like weather, like the actual weather of a specific and terrible summer. And the right Frida, the one in Tehuana dress holding the portrait so carefully, was not simply the stronger self. She was the one who still believed in him.

"But they remarried," Lilianne said. "The following year. So the whole bleeding-heart thing, she took him back."

"That's the part I can't make fit," Jessica admitted. She turned the scrap of paper over, as if the back might hold the rest of the label. "My deposition reads like it's final. She testifies that she's bleeding out. And then a year later she changes her testimony." Bree laughed and said that sounded like every breakup she'd ever watched, and Lilianne said the painting could still be true even if it turned out not to last, the way a photograph of rain is still true even after the sun comes back.

Mr. Nkosi was stacking chairs, and Jessica almost asked him which of them was right, whether the painting counted as evidence of loss or of survival. Instead she copied the dates into her notebook, under her marginal note about the vein, and looked once more at the two women holding hands in the middle of the storm, each carrying the other's pulse. "She painted it in the middle," Jessica said, mostly to the poster. "Not before, not after. In the middle." She put the cap on her pen and started helping stack the chairs.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The InVID-WeVerify browser plugin, built by a European Union-funded project, splits a video into key frames that can be reverse-searched.
story:
The video arrived at his grandfather's phone the way these things always did, forwarded twice before it reached him, captioned in capital letters. Eric watched it over his shoulder in the kitchen: floodwater tearing through a street, a man clinging to a car door, a crowd screaming behind a camera that shook and steadied and shook again. His grandfather's thumb hovered above the forward arrow. "Send that to your mother," he said. "She should see what's happening out there."

Eric had spent the previous Wednesday at his mother's office, filling out housing forms on a spare desk while she was in meetings. A colleague named Amelie had leaned over his shoulder while he scrolled, watched him pause on a similar clip, and asked whether he meant to share it. When he said probably, she pulled a chair over. "Before you send anything like this, try this," she said, and installed something called InVID-WeVerify in his browser. It had come out of a European Union-funded project, she told him, and it split a video into key frames that could be reverse-searched. She clicked one frame, dropped it into a search bar, and an older news article surfaced beside the new one, same image, different year. He had felt something shift in him then, a small emancipation from the reflex he hadn't known he had, the reflex to pass things along.

He had not thought about it again until now, in his grandfather's kitchen, with the smell of toast and the diurnal ritual of the morning paper still folded on the table, obsolete in a way neither of them would say aloud. "Hold on," Eric said. "Before you send it. Give me one minute." His grandfather's thumb stayed where it was, patient but skeptical, the skepticism of a man who had believed newspapers for sixty years and now believed everything that reached his phone with equal confidence.

Eric fetched his laptop and opened the video's page. The plugin's icon sat in the corner of the browser where Amelie had left it. He pasted the link and waited, conscious of his grandfather breathing behind him, of the kettle beginning its low complaint. The screen divided. The video had been broken into still images, one after another, like film laid out on a lightbox. Key frames, the interface called them, and Eric understood without being told that these were the bones of the thing, the parts that could be checked.

He chose the clearest frame, the one showing a storefront sign half-submerged, and reverse-searched it. Results loaded. At first nothing matched, and he felt the small humiliation of a person who has made a fuss. His grandfather said, "See, it's real, it's happening." Braden had already texted Eric the same video an hour ago, and Eric had almost forwarded it to his own group chat before breakfast, wanting to be the one who'd seen it first. That want was still in him, coiled somewhere under the patience.

He tried a second frame, the man on the car door. This time the search returned a news site in a language he couldn't read, dated years earlier. Then a second article. Then a fact-checking page with the same still image at the top, and beneath it a date, and beneath the date a place neither of them had been. The flood was real. The flood was not now, and it was not where the caption said, and the man on the car door had probably climbed down and dried off and gone on with his life while his image drowned again and again in other people's feeds.

His grandfather put the phone on the table, screen down. He looked at the laptop, then at the window, where the actual day was proceeding ordinary and dry. "So it's a lie," he said. Eric hesitated. It wasn't exactly a lie, and it wasn't exactly true, and he could feel both of those ideas refusing to collapse into each other. "It's an old thing wearing new clothes," he said finally. "Someone wants people upset." He thought of his history teacher, Mr. Fraser, who had once written the word relativism on the board and then crossed it out, saying some things are just wrong, and Eric had agreed then and half-agreed now, because the video was wrong but the flood had happened, somewhere, to someone, and that mattered too.

"Would you have sent it?" his grandfather asked. "Before you knew the trick with the frames." Eric was quiet long enough for the kettle to click off. "I almost sent it this morning," he said. "Barely even checked. And I knew how to check." He could still feel the pull of the forward arrow, the little reward of being early with bad news, and he did not know whether the plugin had cured that or only delayed it. His grandfather picked up his phone again and turned it over in his hands, once, twice. "Show me," he said. "Show me how you did it."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
story:
The kitchen table still smelled of the onion her mother had chopped an hour before, and Victoria spread her worksheet over the spot where the cutting board had been. Question four had a diagram of two parallel plates, 0.02 metres apart, with 100 volts across them, and asked for the field strength at a point in between. In the margin, her own handwriting said 50, circled twice, then crossed out.

She remembered the moment she'd written it. Ms. Mendoza had returned the quizzes at the end of class on Friday, and Victoria had watched the paper land face-down on her desk, the way you watch weather arrive. She'd gotten everything right except this one, and she had flipped back through her notes on the bus, feeling a low foreboding that the mistake was simple and therefore worse. Two centimetres divided into 100 volts. Fifty. It had looked so reasonable.

Her phone buzzed against the table. Libby had sent a photo of her own worksheet, question four blank, and beneath it: did you get it? i trust you more than the textbook.

Victoria pulled the plates diagram closer. The answer she'd given was a hundred times too small, she realized now, because she'd divided by the distance in centimetres instead of metres. She said it aloud to the empty kitchen, just to hear it. "It wants metres." Her voice sounded flat against the humming refrigerator. She tried again with the numbers as given, 100 volts across 0.02 metres, and wrote 5,000, and then the units, volts per metre, which Ms. Mendoza had made them chant once, volts per metre, like a train station call. Five thousand volts per metre between the plates.

not yet, she typed to Libby. im redoing it. She set the phone face-down, which was a habit her mother called rude and which Victoria preferred to think of as temporary, a small door closed until she could open it again.

From the living room her mother was on the phone with her sister, saying the word phenotypic the way she said all her nursing words, worn smooth from use. "The phenotypic differences between the twins," her mother was saying, "they don't tell you what's going to happen, they tell you what's already shown up." Victoria wrote that down in the margin of her worksheet without deciding to, under the crossed-out fifty. She wasn't sure yet why it belonged with the plates, only that it did, the way two numbers side by side could.

Braden had texted earlier, a voice memo she hadn't played. He'd been the one who leaned over her desk on Friday and said, quietly, "You too? I put fifty." A hundred times too small, and he'd seemed almost glad to have company in it, which had bothered her more than the mark itself. She played the memo now. His voice filled the kitchen, tinny and close. "Anyway," he was saying, "I figure one question doesn't predicate the whole grade, right? Like it's one question out of fifty points. Text me if you figure out what we did."

She looked at the diagram again. At a point in between, the question said, as if the point were a place you could stand. She thought of standing between the plates, which was ridiculous, and then thought about how the field was the same everywhere in between, five thousand volts per metre whether the point was near the top plate or the bottom or exactly centered. That was the part that had seemed too easy when she'd first read it, and now it seemed like the part that was actually true, and she couldn't have said which of those two impressions she trusted.

She typed to Libby: its 5,000 volts per metre. i got it wrong the first time because i used the centimetres. dont do that. Then she sat with her thumb over send, because telling Libby meant admitting she'd been wrong, and Libby had said i trust you more than the textbook.

Her mother came in for water, still on the phone, and touched Victoria's shoulder in passing without breaking her sentence. The glass filled. The tap squeaked off.

Victoria sent the message, then played Braden's memo a second time, and started a reply: we divided by centimetres. She stopped there, holding the phone, the kitchen light buzzing faintly above the two plates on the page.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
Anna spread the textbook across the picnic table in her grandfather's backyard, weighted at the corners with two horseshoes and a cracked mug. The test was Monday, and the chapter was climate science, and the graph she had to memorize rose in a thin, climbing line, carbon dioxide measured every year since before her grandfather was born. Behind her, her cousin Pearl dragged the garden hose across the grass, filling a galvanized tub for the dogs, who watched the water rise with total indifference.

"Sit," Anna said. "Test me."

Pearl dropped the hose, let it spasm on the grass, and sat on the bench across the table. She was staying the week with the grandparents too, and she had already finished her own summer reading, which gave her an air of leisure Anna found faintly insulting. Anna read aloud from her notes: "Explain how greenhouse gases trap heat."

"Easy," Anna said, before Pearl could answer. "The atmosphere lets sunlight in, and the gases trap the heat that radiates back off the ground. And the gases that do the most trapping are the ones there's the most of. Nitrogen and oxygen. They're basically the whole atmosphere, so they're doing the heavy lifting."

Pearl was quiet for a moment, which Anna took for admiration. Then Pearl pulled the textbook toward her and turned pages with a librarian's patience. "Read this part," she said, tapping a paragraph.

Anna read it. Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation. She read it twice, and the second time the words rearranged something in her head, the way a picture looks different once you see the second face hidden in it. The most abundant gases, the ones she breathed without thinking, were exactly the ones that did nothing. The heavy lifting was done by the rare ones, the trace gases, present like salt in soup.

"That's backwards," Anna said. "The whole thing is backwards. The air is almost entirely gases that can't trap heat at all."

"Molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation," Pearl said, like she was reciting it for her own amusement. "So says the book."

The screen door banged and their grandfather came out with two glasses of iced tea, the kind that went cloudy where the cold cream coagulated against the ice. He set them down and squinted at the graph Anna had copied onto loose paper, the climbing line reproduced in her own shaky pencil.

"That line," he said. "When I was a boy there was ice on this creek every January. You could walk to school on it. There's an ordinance in this town now about backyard fires, you know. Can't burn leaves after eight o'clock. As if a few leaves matter against that." He tapped the paper, not unkindly, and went back inside, leaving his tea untouched.

Anna stared at her own graph. The line rose, and rose, and the whole century was in it, her grandfather's creek in it somewhere, and hers too, somewhere past the edge of the paper where the graph stopped but the line, she understood, did not. She had wanted the test to be a thing she could finish, a chapter she could close, and now it wasn't. The trace gases were few and the effect was large, and the graph was simple and the world it measured was not, and she could hold both of those facts only by holding them loosely.

"Ask me again," Anna said. "From the start."

Pearl asked. Anna answered, carefully, the sunlight in, the infrared out, the trace gases absorbing what the abundant ones could not, and she got it right this time, every part of it, and Pearl nodded and said, "You'd pass." Anna looked at the grass, at the roses her grandmother claimed were autochthonous to this county, growing where they had always grown, no help needed. Somewhere past the fence the creek ran low and dark in the August heat.

"So," Pearl said, coiling the hose. "You know it now."

"I know the part that's on the test," Anna said. She folded the graph in half, and in half again, and put it in her pocket, where she could feel its edge against her leg all afternoon.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Truman Doctrine, announced in March 1947, pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure, starting with aid to Greece and Turkey.
story:
The archive smelled of paper that had outlived the people who wrote it, and Adam had already decided this was better than any library he'd ever been in. He spread his materials across the long table beneath the tall windows: two photocopies, one from a historian named Fossedal who argued the Cold War began the moment Truman stood before Congress, and one from a scholar named Priya who put the start earlier, in a diplomat's long-winded cable sent from Moscow the year before. Mr. Sutton, the archivist, had warned him not to dog-ear anything, and Adam had felt the rectitude of that rule settle over him like a uniform, though he wasn't sure why obeying it made him feel so serious.

He was there because of an argument, the kind that starts small and then takes over your week. On Sunday, at his grandfather's apartment, Adam had been taping a timeline across the living room wall, a school project stretching from 1945 to 1962, when Jaydon, who had come over ostensibly to help but mostly to eat the grandfather's crackers, had planted himself in front of the blank space before 1947 and said, "You should start it there. That's when it actually started." Adam had asked him where, exactly, and Jaydon had tapped the wall. "The Truman Doctrine. March 1947. Truman pledged support for countries resisting communist pressure. Greece and Turkey first." Their grandfather, from his chair, had said only, "Or the telegram," and refused to elaborate, which was his way of starting arguments he could then watch.

Now Adam had come to the city archive to collate the evidence himself, because both explanations had begun to seem true and that felt like a problem. Priya's essay claimed the Long Telegram of 1946 had already framed the Soviets as an implacable opponent, making everything after it inevitable paperwork. Fossedal claimed that a diplomat's pessimism was only opinion until a president committed money and policy to it, and that commitment came with the doctrine. Adam read each page twice, then lined them side by side like two witnesses to the same accident who remembered different cars.

Brianna arrived at noon with a bag of clementines and the confidence of someone who had done her essay the week it was assigned. "You're still on the start date," she said, peeling one. "Nobody's grading your philosophy, they're grading your timeline." She leaned over the table, and Adam noticed how her eyes moved down Fossedal's page the way his did, faster at first, then slower at the good parts, and he wondered whether everyone read like that, sprinting and then wading. "But if you have to pick one," she said, "pick the one with a document you can touch."

Mr. Sutton passed with a cart of grey boxes and paused at their table. He didn't lecture, which Adam appreciated; he only set down a folder marked 1947 and said, "Congressional record, if it helps," and moved on. Adam opened it. There was the speech, or the record of it, Truman before Congress in March 1947, and there, in print, the pledge: support for countries resisting communist pressure, aid to Greece, aid to Turkey. He had known the words from Jaydon's mouth on Sunday; now he knew them from the page, and they felt different on the page, heavier, as if the paper itself had been asked to carry the money.

He sat back and tried to hold both accounts at once, the way you hold two wet stones, one in each hand. Priya's reading made the doctrine a consequence, a river reaching a point it had been flowing toward. Fossedal's made it a hinge, the moment opinion hardened into commitment. What would it mean for both to be partly right? That a feeling became a fact in March 1947 but had been a feeling for a year before that, circulating through the State Department like a rumour nobody had yet paid for? He wrote in his notebook: start of the war, or start of the war being official? Then he crossed out "official" because it wasn't quite right and he didn't have a better word.

"So which is it?" Brianna asked, dropping a peel into her bag. "The speech or the telegram?"

"I don't know yet," Adam said, and was surprised by how little this bothered him. "The telegram made the argument. The doctrine made it policy. Depending on what you think a war is, either one could be the start." He tapped the congressional record. "This is the first time the country itself said it, though. Out loud, in front of Congress, with Greece and Turkey attached to it." He liked how pithy the speech was, given what it set in motion; a few sentences and the map changed.

Brianna shrugged and stole his pen to write March 1947 on his timeline strip, in the space before which Jaydon had argued nothing mattered. Adam let her, but in his notebook he drew a dotted line backwards from that date to a small mark labelled 1946, and between them he wrote, in smaller letters, the thing he couldn't yet prove: that the ground had shifted before anyone announced it.

At closing time Mr. Sutton came to collect the folder, and Adam asked, quietly, whether the archive kept diplomats' cables too. Mr. Sutton considered him for a moment, then said the Moscow files were three aisles over, closed on Sundays. Adam packed his timeline into the tube he'd brought, and Brianna held the door, and outside the evening had gone cold and blue over the bus stop across the street.

"I'm coming back Sunday anyway," Adam said.

Brianna zipped her bag. "Grandpa's going to love that."

"He started it," Adam said, and stepped off the curb.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: Google added 'search by image' in 2011, letting users upload a picture or paste its link to find where else it appears on the web.
story:
Kingsley's kitchen smelled of burnt toast and dish soap, and Felicia had claimed the last unbroken chair, so Zachary sat on the counter with his phone balanced on his knee. They were supposed to be outlining a history essay, though so far the outline consisted of Felicia's argument that the whole assignment was pointless and Kingsley's counter-argument that complaining about it was also pointless. Then Zachary's phone buzzed and his grandmother's name came up with a photo attached: a street turned into a river, a man on a roof holding a hand-lettered sign that read HELP US, water the color of weak tea swallowing a row of parked cars.

The message underneath said, "This is forty minutes from your school. Please be careful. Forwarding to everyone." Then a second message, three praying hands emojis and the words "Pass it on so people know."

Zachary zoomed in. Something about the light bothered him, the long autumn shadows, though he couldn't have said why. "Guys," he said, and held out the phone. "My grandma sent this. Says it's near our school."

Kingsley leaned over Felicia's shoulder to look. "That's not near our school. That looks like the flood pictures from years ago, the ones they rerun every hurricane season."

"Then why does she think it's now?" Felicia took the phone, tilted the screen. "Somebody's captioning old stuff like it's breaking news. That's so grim."

Zachary had a vague memory of his mother, one exhausted evening, saying you could look a picture up backwards, that the internet had made a whole machinery for checking where a thing had been. He'd half listened, the way he half listened to most of his mother's injunctions about the phone. He took the phone back and typed into the search bar: how to find where a photo came from.

The results came up fast. The top ones explained that Google had added search by image back in 2011, so you could take a picture you had and upload it, or paste in a link to it, and see where else on the web the same picture had turned up. It felt almost too simple. He copied the image address from his grandmother's message, pasted it into the image search box, and hit enter.

The page filled with thumbnails. The roof, the man, the sign, the tea-colored water, over and over, and beside each one a date. 2015. 2015. 2016, shared during a different flood, with a different state in the caption. One page, a fact-checking site, had the original photographer's name and the actual date the water had come through that particular street, five years and six hundred miles from anything near his school. The image had been beguiling, Zachary thought, in the way that made it travel: a man on a roof, a plea in marker, no context necessary. The caption was the only new part, and the caption was the lie.

"Whoa," Felicia said, reading over his arm. "So it's just been circulating for years. People keep dressing it up."

"So do I tell her?" Zachary was already scrolling to his grandmother's contact. "She sent it to everyone. Like, everyone, her whole church list."

"If you don't, who does?" Kingsley said. He said it lightly, nonchalant, already turning back to the essay outline, but the question sat in Zachary's chest like a swallowed stone. His grandmother was not a stupid woman. She had run a payroll office for thirty years; she caught arithmetic errors other people missed. But a photograph did not feel like arithmetic. A photograph felt like seeing.

He called her instead of texting. She picked up on the second ring, TV murmuring behind her, and he talked her through it, the image search, pasting the link, and she was quiet while he explained that the picture was real but old, that the man had been rescued, that the water near his school was just ordinary November rain. "Well," she said at last, and he could hear her settling into something. "Well. I sent it to sixty people, Zachary." A pause. "Show me again how you did that. The pasting part. Slowly."

He talked her through it once more, the uploading and the link, and she repeated the steps back to him like a recipe she intended to keep. When he hung up, Felicia had written three actual points on the essay outline and Kingsley was scraping the black off a second round of toast. Zachary texted his grandmother a link to the fact-check page so she'd have it in writing, then sat looking at the empty search box, at the machinery that was there, had been there since he was four years old, waiting for him to use it. There would be another photo, probably by Friday. He might not catch the next one either. But he had the steps now, and so did she, and sixty people in her church list had gotten a second message that began, "Correction, from Zachary."

"All right," Felicia said, spinning the outline to face him. "You're on the third body paragraph. And put your phone down."

Zachary put the phone face-down on the counter and picked up the pen.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Albert Mehrabian's often-quoted '7 percent words, 38 percent tone, 55 percent face' rule came from experiments on conveying feelings, and he said it does not apply to all communication.
story:
Elijah had the statistic saved as a screenshot on his phone since October. It said that words carried only 7 percent of a message, while tone carried 38 percent and the face carried 55 percent. He had found it at one in the morning, in a rabbit hole of job interview tips, and it had coagulated there, at the bottom of everything he believed about the coming Saturday, when he would sit across a desk from the manager of the garden centre and try to be hired.

On Thursday afternoon he stood in the doorway of the school library, where Maryam was shelving returns for her community service block. "I've decided the answers don't matter," he said. "Seven percent. I can say basically anything as long as I look right."

Maryam slid a book about freshwater fish into its place and looked at him. "Where'd you get that?"

"Some study. Albert Mehrabian. Seven, thirty-eight, fifty-five. It's famous."

"It's famous for being wrong about that," she said. She pulled out her own phone, typed, and turned the screen toward him. "Those numbers came from experiments about conveying feelings. He said it doesn't apply to all communication. It's on record."

Elijah read the small text twice. He did not argue, but he did not update either, not fully. The numbers still felt useful, the way a coin feels useful even after you learn it isn't lucky.

That evening he practised in the bathroom mirror, and his father walked past and said he looked like he was being interrogated. Elijah tried again, softer, and his father said he looked like he was apologizing for something. "Which one gets me the job?" Elijah called after him, and his father laughed from the hallway and did not answer.

On Friday, Jiya cornered him outside the gym. Jiya had interviewed at the bakery in September and been hired on the spot, and she held this over everyone the way a chess player holds a won position. "Say your answer about why you want the job," she demanded.

"I'm hardworking, dependable, and I love plants."

"You don't love plants."

"I love money that plants produce."

"Say that," Jiya said. "Say it exactly like that, to her face, and hold eye contact." Elijah tried, and Jiya shook her head. "You went blase halfway through. Like the words were beneath you. You're doing the thing where you decide the words are only seven percent so you stop caring about them, and it shows."

"That's not what seven percent means," Elijah said, but even as he said it he could hear the flaw. If tone and face carried the rest, then a lazy face betrayed lazy words. The statistic didn't set the words free. It chained them to everything else.

He sat on the bench outside the gym for a while after Jiya went in to change. Maryam's fact and Jiya's fact seemed to point in opposite directions, one saying words were nearly nothing and one saying they were everything, and he turned them over until they settled into something he could actually use: the words had to be true and specific, and the face and voice would carry whether the words were true. The uncertainty that remained was which half of him the manager would actually see, and he let that stay uncertain, because there was no way to rehearse a stranger.

On Saturday the garden centre smelled of wet soil and cut pine. The manager was a broad woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and the desk between them held a mound of seed packets waiting to be sorted. She asked the question about why he wanted the job.

"I don't love plants," Elijah said. "I love the work, and I need the money, and I'll show up even when it's raining." He kept his eyes on hers while he said it, which was harder than the sentence.

She sorted three seed packets before responding. "Last kid told me he loved plants. Couldn't tell a spade from a trowel."

"I can't either," Elijah said. "Yet."

The glasses came down out of her hair and onto her nose. She wrote something in the margin of a form, and the pen moved, and outside the window a man in an orange vest watered a row of pines against a grey sky. "Saturdays, eight o'clock," she said. "Wear boots."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: An equilibrium is dynamic: the forward and reverse reactions keep happening, but at equal rates, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
story:
The garage smelled of oil and cut grass, because Carlos had been mowing lawns all morning and had come straight to Mathis's house without showering, an arrangement Sonny had protested with an injunction delivered from the far end of the folding table: sit downwind or sit outside. They sat outside, more or less, the garage door rolled up to let the July heat lean in anyway. Between them lay three highlighters, a bag of salt-and-vinegar chips, and a photocopy of the exam review sheet Ms. Oyelaran had handed out on the last day of term, the one question circled twice in red: predict the effect of a temperature change on a system at equilibrium.

Mathis read it aloud for the fourth time, then set the paper down on the warm concrete. "I don't get what she wants. If you heat it, the reaction goes one way. If you cool it, it goes the other. Fine. But why does it go back to being steady afterward? What's it doing while it's steady? Nothing? Then why call it dynamic?"

"Because she likes words that hurt," Carlos said, and reached across Sonny for the chips.

Sonny, who had failed the midterm and had since become grimly devoted to the subject, flipped his notebook to a page dense with arrows. "It's like my uncle's shop. Hardware store, the one on Delmore. All afternoon the same twelve guys are in there, leaning on the counter, drinking the free coffee. Guys leave, but new guys come in, and it's always about twelve. From outside it looks like nothing's happening. Inside, it never stops."

Mathis looked at him. "Where did you get that?"

"Made it up just now. Two weeks ago it would've been about a bodega, but I've been desensitized. Everything is chemistry to me now. I saw my mom's coffee pot yesterday and thought, heterogeneous mixture."

Carlos laughed hard enough to knock over one highlighter, and Mathis laughed too, but he kept hold of the idea, turning it the way he turned a bolt when he couldn't tell if it was loosening. Same twelve guys. People leaving, people arriving, the count fixed. Forward and reverse, both running, rates equal, amounts constant. That was why it was called dynamic and not dead. "So equilibrium isn't a stop," he said slowly. "It's a tie."

The tie mattered, Sonny argued, because the exam would ask what happens when you break it. He pointed at the review sheet. "Temperature change. You heat it, you're adding energy, and the reaction treats energy like another reactant or another product, depending on which direction releases it. Heat the system and it shifts the way that soaks the heat up. Cool it and it shifts the way that gives heat off." He said it like a man reciting a parole statement, and Mathis suspected he had it memorized without understanding it, the way Sonny had once memorized the entire roster of a hockey team he'd never watched.

They tested it on each other with the old engine block in the corner, the one Mathis's father kept promising to sell. Carlos invented problems: "Blue stuff, clear stuff, forward makes heat. You crank the heat. Go." Mathis worked each one aloud, and when he got one wrong, which he did twice, Sonny made him redo it from the beginning, his voice virulent with triumph. "You said shift left. It goes right. Right, Mathis. The heat is a product, so adding product pushes it backward." Mathis changed his mind the honest way, not grudgingly: he saw it. Once you stopped imagining the reaction as a thing that finished and started imagining it as a room full of people trading places, the direction of the push became almost obvious.

What stayed unobvious, and bothered him on the walk to the store for cold drinks, was the part nobody's uncle's shop could cover. Twelve guys is twelve guys, but a reaction in a beaker is trillions of molecules, and not one of them knows anything. There's no counter to lean on, no free coffee, no reason. Mathis said this out loud on the way back, the cans sweating in the plastic bag, and Sonny considered it while crushing his empty against the fence. "Then it's better than the shop," he said. "Nobody's in charge and it still balances. Every single time." Carlos called that depressing. Sonny called it beautiful. Mathis, holding the door of the garage open with his hip, thought it was neither, or both, and that Ms. Oyelaran would probably mark that answer wrong.

They studied until the streetlights came on, and when Sonny left he took the notebook with him, tucking it under his arm like something stolen. "If I pass," he said from the driveway, "I'm telling Oyelaran about the hardware store. Word for word." Mathis sat back down at the folding table, picked up the red highlighter, and circled the question a fifth time.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
The living room had been rearranged into a theatre, more or less. Aidan's father had hauled the couch against the window, and in its place two strips of painter's tape ran parallel across the carpet, delimiting an imaginary proscenium. Beyond the tape, three kitchen chairs stood in for the set of the one-act he was supposed to direct, and Nikola sat in one of them with the script rolled in his fist like a subpoena.

"From the top," Aidan said, and tapped his pencil against the arm of the recliner he'd claimed as a director's chair.

Nikola rose and delivered his first line to the bookshelf. Sahana, waiting by the fireplace for her entrance, mouthed along with him. It was the third Sunday of rehearsal and the blocking still had the stiffness of furniture being moved by strangers. Aidan watched and wondered why that was, whether a scene had a natural shape the way water had a natural level, and whether his job was to find it or to impose one.

"Cross upstage on that line," he called, because he'd read the term the night before in a handbook from the library, and it had felt good in his mouth, professional.

Nikola turned around, squinting. "Up? The floor's flat. Why is the back of the stage up?"

"I don't know yet," Aidan said, which was true, and it bothered him more than he let on. He'd used a word he couldn't account for. During the break he sat on the stairs with the handbook open across his knees and found the passage, and read it twice, and then a third time with the particular somnolence of Sunday afternoons pressed back by small discovery. When Sahana came over with her mug of tea, he looked up. "Old stages were raked. They sloped down toward the audience. So upstage means away from the audience, downstage toward it."

"That's backwards from how it sounds," she said.

"Only if you're thinking of a map." He turned the handbook over in his hands. "It's thinking of a hill."

The problem surfaced after the break, and it was a real one. Nikola wanted to play his big confrontation standing centre, facing out, and the confrontation was undeniably big. Sahana argued that if he stayed upstage of her the whole scene, she was left acting to the side of his head. "I can't have a fight with an ear," she said. They both looked at Aidan, and he understood that whatever he said next would decide whether he was directing this play or merely hosting it.

He tried the scene both ways, because he wanted to see rather than decide. With Nikola planted centre, the argument was loud and flat, all volume, no geometry. Then he asked Nikola to begin upstage, near the bookshelf, and drift downstage as the truth came out, so that the audience would watch a man descending toward them whether he wanted to or not. It was, he had to admit, a borrowed idea; he'd read something like it, and he couldn't say how much of the choice was his. Maybe none of it. Maybe directing was mostly borrowing well.

"Better?" Nikola asked, when they'd run it twice.

"Better for the audience," Sahana said, which was not the same as better for Nikola, and the three of them knew it. Nikola liked centre. It was where he felt watched, and being watched was most of why he'd auditioned.

Aidan thought about Mr. Goldberg, who taught drama at the school and had told him, the day he handed over the one-act, that a director's real material was attention. He hadn't understood it then. He thought he understood it now: the raked stage, the slope that pulled a body toward the audience, was just a machine for attention, and blocking was its replacement on a flat floor, a way of moving eyes instead of gravity. But there was a second thing pulling too, the actors' own want to be seen, and it didn't always agree with the scene's want. He couldn't have said which one ought to win. He filed the question next to the others he was accumulating, the ones that didn't fit in the handbook.

They ran the scene once more. Nikola began far upstage, by the bookshelf, and came down the invisible slope a step at a time, and Sahana turned with him so that the two of them folded toward the audience together, like something ductile warming in the hands. The last line landed, and for a moment nobody in the living room moved.

"Same time next Sunday?" Nikola said, already reaching for his shoes.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid with a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, pointing to a growing need for schools and teachers.
story:
Nolan's laptop showed two countries side by side, and his father hovered behind him with a mug that read World's Okayest Accountant. The kitchen smelled of burnt toast because Nolan had tried to make eggs while reading and had metabolized neither the eggs nor the reading, judging by the pan soaking in the sink.

"You're still on that volunteer thing?" his father asked.

"The application asks which site you'd be more useful at," Nolan said. "Nursing home in one place, building classrooms in the other. They want a paragraph on why."

"Can't you just pick whichever has better food?"

Nolan tilted the screen away from him. His father raised the mug in surrender and went to the porch, where the evening was doing its slow fade from orange to nothing. That left Nolan alone with the two shapes on the screen, which Mr. Walker, his geography teacher, called population pyramids, though only one of them looked like a pyramid at all.

The first one did: a wide base, narrowing as it climbed, like a sandcastle drip. The second was more of a barrel, fat in the middle, thinner at the bottom. He'd copied both into a document and, under them, written three lines he'd already deleted twice. The application was due at midnight and it was already eight.

He texted Zain, who was theoretically doing the same application, and Zain called him within a minute, which meant he'd been procrastinating too.

"Did you figure out the shapes?" Nolan asked.

"I figured out that I'm choosing based on vibes," Zain said. "Also my mom says hi and do you want the leftover curry, she made too much."

"Tell her yes. The shapes, Zain."

There was the sound of Zain chewing, which meant he was eating while claiming he hadn't started. "Okay, so the one that actually looks like a pyramid has all the people at the bottom, right? Young people. Lots of them. That's the whole thing, that's the base."

"So what does that mean for where you'd build?" Nolan pulled the first pyramid closer, the one with the wide base and the narrow top. If most of the population was crammed into the youngest bars, then in ten years those bars would be teenagers, and after that, workers, and somewhere in there they would need somewhere to learn. He typed: a wide base and narrow top shows a high birth rate and a young population, which points to a growing need for schools and teachers. He stared at it, waiting to doubt it, and didn't.

"Classrooms," Zain said, at the same moment Nolan said it. "Obviously classrooms. The other one's got the fat middle, all the old folks stacked up top, they'll need the nursing home eventually."

"Eventually," Nolan said slowly. "But that's the part I can't figure out. The classroom country needs schools. The barrel country needs nursing homes. And they're asking me, a sixteen-year-old who failed the toast this evening, to rank future strangers' needs."

"You're overthinking. It's a volunteer application, not a plutocracy. They just want to see you can read a graph."

"That's not what plutocracy means."

"It's a rich-people thing, whatever. Come over, I'll give you the curry, we'll finish together."

Nolan looked at his half-written paragraph, then at the pan in the sink, then out at the porch where his father sat with the okayest mug, watching the street like it might do something. He carried the laptop over and set it on the railing.

"Read this," he said.

His father read it, lips moving slightly, an accountant's habit. "This true?"

"That's what the shape shows. Wide base, young population, they'll need teachers. I think."

"You think or you know?"

"Both, kind of." Nolan heard himself say it and decided not to take it back. "The graph part I know. The part where I say a classroom matters more than a nursing home, that I'm choosing. Somebody old in the barrel country needs care now, and some kid in the pyramid country needs a school in five years, and I've got one paragraph."

His father was quiet for the length of a car passing. "When you applied to that math camp last year, you wrote that you weren't sure you deserved it. Remember what happened?"

"I got in anyway."

"You got in anyway." He tapped the screen. "So write it with the doubt in it. The doubt's not a hole, it's just honest."

Nolan went back inside and rewrote the paragraph twice. The final version said the pyramid country's shape pointed to schools and teachers, and that he chose the classroom site, and that he understood the choice left the other need unmet by him, though not by everyone. He read it over once, decided it was the truest thing he could manage by midnight, and hit submit before he could metabolize second thoughts.

Then he put on his shoes, took the container his mother had left by the door for the curry exchange, and walked the six blocks to Zain's house, where the porch light was on and Zain was already outside, holding the Tupperware like a trophy.

"It's turgid with lentils," Zain said. "That's a compliment to the lentils."

"You still don't know what that means either."

"Trade you it for your paragraph."

Nolan handed over his phone, took the curry, and stood there in the dark while his best friend read his half-certain answer to the world and nodded slowly, twice, like it was worth something.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
Noah had claimed the corner table by the window because it had the only outlet, and because from there he could watch the maple outside drop its late-April leaves of light across the sidewalk. The arboreal shade moved slowly across his laptop screen while he opened, for the ninth time that week, the portal that still said the same thing. Waitlisted. The word had begun to feel like an oxymoron, soft and brutal at once, a door held open by a foot.

Penelope came in with Charlee behind her, both of them carrying the paper cups that meant they had already been somewhere and were mid-conversation. She set her latte down on his table without asking, which was her way of asking. "Still nothing?"

"Still nothing," Noah said. "They said decisions come whenever they come. Which is not a policy, it's a shrug."

Charlee pulled over a chair. "You haven't paid Whitmore yet, though. The deposit's due Tuesday."

"Two hundred dollars to a school I don't want, to hold a seat I'd abandon the second the other one calls." He closed the laptop halfway, a decision he immediately regretted, because the screen went dark and the room got louder. "And if they never call, I've paid two hundred dollars for nothing."

Penelope stirred her drink. She had done this already, he remembered; she had gotten into her first choice in December, early, no ambiguity anywhere in it. But she said, "My cousin was waitlisted last year. She told me it works like this. The college waits until May. That's when they fill the waitlist spots, because by then the admitted students have sent in their deposits, and the college finally knows how many places are still open."

Noah turned that over. He had been imagining the waitlist as a kind of queue, his name inching forward in real time, and the image had made the waiting feel like his own failure of patience. Instead there was a whole second calendar underneath the one he'd been living by, and nothing could happen on it until May arrived and the deposits landed. "So it's not that they're slow," he said slowly. "They can't know yet. Nobody can."

"Right. She paid a deposit somewhere else anyway, just in case, and lost it. She said that was the price of sleeping."

"That's a terrible system," Charlee said.

"It's an honest one, maybe," Noah said. "You pay to instantiate one possible future and hold a ticket to another. Everybody knows what the money is for." He was talking like it was already decided, and he noticed that, and let it stand.

From the counter, where Ms. Girma had been waiting for a cappuccino, the three of them looked like a small tribunal, heads bent over the table, the boy's laptop half-shut like a book someone meant to return to. She had taught Noah in eleventh grade and knew the particular stillness he got when he was arguing himself out of a position he had just argued himself into. She carried her cup toward the door, then stopped. "Noah. Whatever you decide, decide it before Tuesday, not on Tuesday."

"Yes, Ms. Girma," he said, and she left without waiting to see whether he meant it.

Penelope watched him open the laptop again. She had known him since they were fourteen, and she knew that his problem was never the deciding; it was that he wanted the deciding to be permanent, wanted every choice to close like a well-made door. "You could pay the deposit," she said, "and stay on the waitlist, and let both things be true for a few weeks. You're allowed to have it both ways for a while."

"That's the part I hate."

"I know," she said. "That's the part everybody hates."

Charlee had drifted toward the window and was squinting at the maple, at the small green beetles climbing its trunk in a line so straight it looked drawn on. "Hey, Noah. If you end up at Whitmore, this tree's still here. It's not going anywhere."

Noah looked at the tree, then at the portal's blue login screen, then at the calendar app where Tuesday sat, boxed and unremarkable, three days away. He pulled his bank card out of his wallet and set it on the table beside Penelope's cup, and left it there, faceup, while he typed his password in.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: A binary search of one million sorted items needs at most 20 comparisons, because halving one million twenty times leaves a single item.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of burnt insulation and floor wax, and the bleachers held more people than Noah's whole school. Their robot, a squat thing with treads and a forklift arm, sat dead on the practice table while the queue of inspection teams shuffled past. Somewhere in its code, buried under three hundred lines Noah had written at two in the morning, a loop was dragging through a lookup table of calibration values, a million sorted entries, checking each one in order from the top. The robot had a ninety-second window to find its target and it had used forty of them just deciding where it was.

"Your loop is the problem," Walker said, tapping the laptop screen with a plastic fork from the concession stand. "I timed it. It's reading that table like a guy reading a phone book from page one."

"Then it reads fast," Noah said, but he didn't believe it, and Walker's fork kept hovering over the same six lines of code like it was adjudicating a dispute between them and had already chosen a side.

Madden, who had spent the morning losing a staring contest with the team from the technical magnet school, leaned over the other shoulder. He was the one who suggested the race. He pulled up the table on his own laptop, typed a target value into a script, and said, "You go in order. I'll do something else. Loser buys the pizza." Noah liked Madden's way of making a problem into a contest, though he had begun to suspect, that spring, that Madden did it mostly to watch other people lose. There was a word for somebody like that, a word Ms. Kaya had once used about a character in a novel, and it had stuck with Noah because it fit so many people he knew: egoist.

Noah's script ground forward, ten thousand entries, forty thousand, and Madden did something Noah couldn't see, folded the table in half and then in half again, each fold a motion of the wrist, until the screen blinked and printed a number. Madden had found it in twenty comparisons. Noah's script was still under two hundred thousand. He let it run to the end anyway, out of a stubbornness he wasn't proud of, and the final count came to over six hundred thousand. A million sorted items, twenty comparisons, if you kept halving. He said it out loud to be sure he'd heard himself right, and Madden nodded around a mouthful of the fork Walker had abandoned.

Ms. Kaya came by with a clipboard and a face like weather about to turn choleric, and when Noah showed her the numbers she only looked at the screen for a long moment and then at him. "So what are you going to do about it," she said, which was not a question, and walked on toward the inspection table. Noah rewrote the search with the halving idea, testing the midpoint, discarding half, again and again. He called it what it was, out loud, half to himself: "Binary search." His fingers smelled of solder and his back ached from folding into a plastic chair for six hours, and outside the gymnasium doors the afternoon light had gone the color of weak tea, which meant the qualifier rounds were close.

The robot ran. It found its calibration value almost instantly, swung to the target zone, and stacked its crate in a time that put them second on the board. Madden whooped and Walker clapped him on the shoulder so hard the laptop nearly slid off the table. Noah watched the ranking screen and felt the clean click of something understood, the whole shape of it, halving a million items down to one, and he thought about how much of the year he had spent doing everything the slow way and calling it thoroughness.

Then the score dropped to fourth, and then to sixth, as other teams ran. The last team, the one from the magnet school, beat their time by four seconds, and Madden went quiet in a way Noah had never seen. On the bus home, in the dark that smelled of heater dust, Walker admitted what he'd found while repacking the crate: the reason their early runs had timed out wasn't the search at all. A battery connector had been loose the whole morning, cutting power to the treads, and it had seated itself properly sometime around lunch. The slow loop had never actually been the thing that failed them.

Noah sat with that the whole ride, the fix in his pocket that had worked, that was true, that had mattered, and that also might not have mattered at all. He couldn't make those two facts sit together. Madden's phone lit up from the seat across the aisle, showing the magnet school's coach shaking the winning student's hand, and Madden turned the screen off and looked out the window. "Next year," Madden said, "I'm reading the phone book from the middle."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Amelia had chosen her shoes before Dylan arrived, which she considered a small victory, because it meant she would not have to choose anything while he was watching. The bowling alley smelled of rented leather and disinfectant, and the overhead lights turned everyone's skin the same faint blue. She stood at lane twelve with a ball she had picked for its weight, not its colour, and practised looking casual against the ball return.

Dylan came in shaking rain off his jacket, and he said something about the weather being bellicose, all wind and threats, and she laughed harder than the joke deserved because laughing was easier than speaking. He was in her chemistry class, two rows over, and until Thursday he had been a person she summarised in a single thought. Then he had asked, quietly, while they both waited for the photocopies, whether she wanted to do something this weekend, and she had said yes before she had finished hearing the question.

The first game went badly for both of them, which helped. He bowled two gutters in a row and made a face like a man betrayed by his own wrist, and Amelia knocked down seven pins and then one, slowly, as if the tenth were a private decision. By the second game she had stopped performing and started playing, and her throws got cleaner, and she noticed his got cleaner too, the way people mirror each other without deciding to.

"Best of three?" he asked when the second game ended with her ahead by eleven.

She agreed, and the third game turned serious in a way neither of them had planned. He pulled ahead in the sixth frame; she pulled even in the eighth; and by the tenth they were tied, and the whole lane seemed to narrow to the seven pins standing between them and a result. Her heart was going hard enough that she could feel it in her throat. She picked up the ball, wiped her palm on her jeans, and told herself it was only bowling, and did not believe herself at all.

Her final throw wobbled and clipped the head pin, and four fell, and Dylan needed three to win and got five. He raised both arms like a tournament champion, and someone at the snack counter clapped once, ironically, and Dylan bowed to her, and Amelia laughed, and her heart was still hammering, and she looked at him across the lane and thought, there it is. That feeling. That must be the feeling.

She was quiet on the walk to the counter for fries, and he asked twice whether she was okay, and she prevaricated, saying she was tired, saying the shoes pinched, saying the noise was a lot, each excuse thinner than the last. She was not tired and the shoes were fine. She was trying to locate a sensation, the way you try to locate a sound in a dark house.

She found Kimberly at the arcade end of the building, feeding quarters to a racing game she had no interest in winning. Kimberly worked Saturdays at the shoe counter and knew the alley's sociology better than anyone, and had opinions on everything like a self-appointed pundit of lane twelve, which Amelia had told her more than once.

"I need to ask you something weird," Amelia said.

"You're blushing," Kimberly said. "This is going to be good."

"After the tiebreaker. My heart was going crazy, and it's still kind of going, and when I looked at Dylan afterwards I felt this, I don't know, pull. And I can't tell if I actually like him or if it's just the game still in my system."

Kimberly turned from the machine, delighted. "Okay, so my cousin took psych last year and she told me about this. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal. When your heart races from fear or excitement, you mistake it for attraction to the person standing next to you."

Amelia repeated the words to herself, misattribution of arousal, and felt something loosen. "So it might not be real."

"Or it might be," Kimberly said. "That's the fun part. The heartbeat doesn't come with a label."

Amelia carried the fries back to the table where Dylan was arranging the ketchup into a small reservoir, precisely, with the tip of a fry. She sat down and ate one and found she was watching his hands, his ridiculous ketchup engineering, the way he looked up mid-drip to see if she had noticed.

She thought about it while he talked about his older brother's car, some saga of a dead battery and a rescue at midnight. The racing heart was evidence of something, that much was true, but evidence of what was a question the body declined to answer. She could not sort the jitters of the tiebreaker from the jitters of sitting here, and she suspected that even the心理学家, whoever they were, could not have sorted it for her from this distance. What she could do was notice both feelings honestly, hold them side by side, and decide not to decide yet.

"There's another open lane," Dylan said, gesturing with the ketchup fry. "Rubber match. I'll even let you pick the ball."

"You had five pins on me," Amelia said, already standing. "Bring the heavy one."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
Nathan had been voted director of the fall one-act on the strength of one argument, made in Mr. Toussaint's drama class, that the play's ending should happen in silence rather than in a speech. He regretted the victory almost immediately. Directing, it turned out, mostly meant standing in the empty auditorium after sixth period while two actors explained to him, in escalating detail, why each of them deserved to stand further downstage.

"The light is better on my side," Tucker said, pointing at the blue wash spilling from the left boom.

"The light is better because I'm standing in it," Hamza said. "That's how light works. It finds talent." He said this with such calm conviction that Nathan laughed before he could stop himself, which cost him a certain amount of authority, like a referee tripping over his own whistle.

Mr. Toussaint had told them almost nothing, which was his method. He had handed Nathan a battered paperback about stage direction, said "You'll figure out where people stand, or you won't," and gone back to arguing with the lighting board. Nathan took the book home and read forty pages about composition and sightlines and the difference between movement that means something and movement that is just furniture rearranging itself. On page sixty-three he found the word he needed, and the next day he brought the book to rehearsal and made Tucker read the passage out loud, partly because Tucker had a good voice for facts and partly because Nathan did not entirely trust himself not to mangle them.

"It's called blocking," Tucker read, "and the word comes from nineteenth-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a miniature stage using a wooden block for each actor." He looked up. "Gilbert. The pirates guy. He moved little blocks around before he moved people."

"So we're blocks," Hamza said. "Finally, a system that recognizes my true shape."

Nathan had been prepared for this to be a hard sell, and was slightly insulted by how easy it wasn't. He spread a scarf across the top of the upright piano in the wings, drew the shape of the stage on it in chalk, and set down a penny for each actor. He had meant it as a private planning trick, something he did before the others arrived, but Tucker and Hamza crowded in as soon as they saw it, and within a minute the three of them were moving pennies with the solemnity of generals. The melancholic ending of the play, which had resisted every attempt at staging for a week, suddenly had a shape: if the penny marked Hamza crossed away from the penny marked Tucker at the moment of the last line, instead of toward him, the whole scene turned from a reconciliation into a departure. It was a colder ending. Nathan liked it more, and felt a small dishonesty in liking it, since he had argued only yesterday for warmth.

The disagreement that followed was not about where to stand, which felt like progress, but about what the play meant, which felt like a trapdoor opening under the progress. Tucker thought the ending should reward the characters, that the whole story was about two people who had earned their way back to each other, that the play was basically a small meritocracy of feeling where effort paid out in forgiveness. Hamza thought that was sentimental garbage, that forgiveness in real life arrived or didn't like weather, regardless of who tried hardest, and that a director who staged it as a reward was lying to the audience with their bodies. Nathan stood between them holding two pennies and understood, with an unpleasant clarity, that the pennies were not the argument. The pennies were only where the argument would have to be settled.

"Both of you," he said. "Run it twice."

They ran it twice. The warm version first: Tucker crossed to Hamza, they stood shoulder to shoulder under the blue wash, and it looked like a commercial for something. Then the cold version: Hamza turned away at the last line, Tucker stayed, and the silence after the line went on a beat too long, which was the first time all week the silence had felt like part of the play instead of an accident of it. Nathan watched from the third row with the chalked scarf still over his arm, and he could not decide, honestly, which one was truer. The book had said the director's job was to decide. The book had not said what to do when deciding felt like choosing between two honest answers.

He made them run it a third time, cold, but with Tucker taking one half-step after Hamza, late, as if following a thought he would probably never finish. Tucker asked whether that was blocking or acting. Nathan said he didn't care what it was called as long as nobody moved the pennies without telling him, and Hamza said, "The meritocracy of pennies," and saluted one of them.

Mr. Toussaint appeared at the back of the house, having apparently noticed that the lighting board was losing the argument on its own. He watched the last run without a word, and when it ended he did not give notes. He only raised his clipboard toward the piano, toward the scarf with its chalk stage and its two worn pennies still standing where the boys had left them.

"Bring the little stage tomorrow," he said. "We're doing act two."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, elevated blood pressure means a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80.
story:
Jade would like it noted, first, that she was not nervous. She had told Aya she wasn't nervous, twice, in the parking lot, and Aya had said "sure" in that laconic way of hers and gone back to her phone. The shadowing placement at Dr. Ferreira's dental practice had come through the health careers program at school, and Ms. Warsame, who ran the program, had said the dentist liked students who showed initiative. Initiative was the whole reason Jade was standing at the front desk at 7:40 in the morning, fifteen minutes early, holding a notebook she had already opened to a blank first page so it would look used.

The first surprise was the blood pressure cuff. Ms. Warsame met her in the waiting room in her hygienist's scrubs and handed her not a chart but a cuff, saying, "We take a reading before anything with anesthesia. You'll do the intake forms today. Ask about somnolence, dizziness, anything on the med list." Jade wrote somnolence down carefully, as though the word might be on a quiz, and followed her back.

The second surprise was her mother. Not literally, at first. The nine o'clock patient was a woman Jade's mother's age, in a cardigan the same faded green, there to have a cracked filling repaired. While Ms. Warsame reviewed the consent form, Jade wrapped the cuff, pressed start, and watched the numbers climb and settle: 125 over 78. She recorded it. It was only when the woman asked, "Is that good? My husband got some number at the pharmacy machine and it said something," that Jade realized she did not know. She had assumed there was a line, good on one side, bad on the other, and she had assumed she would recognize it when she saw it.

"I'll find out," she said, and felt the small fraudulence of it, because she had already told Aya on Tuesday that she "basically knew vitals." Aya wanted this placement for herself, actually. Aya wanted to be a dentist the way other people want to breathe, and she had been waitlisted for the shadowing slot that Jade, who mostly wanted a line on her application that sounded decisive, had gotten. All week Aya had been sending links about enamel and gingivitis, helpful and slightly pointed, like a creditor sending reminders.

The office had a laminated reference sheet taped inside the supply cabinet, and Jade slipped into the back room to read it where no one could see her not knowing. Under the 2017 American guideline, it said, elevated blood pressure meant a systolic reading of 120 to 129 with a diastolic reading below 80. She stood there with the numbers. 125 fell between 120 and 129. 78 was below 80. She checked it twice, the way she checked algebra. So the reading was elevated. Not high, not hypertension, not the emergency she had half imagined. A category she hadn't known existed, sitting in the middle of things.

She came back out and said, quietly, so the woman in the green cardigan could choose whether to hear, "It's in the elevated range." The woman nodded slowly, the way people nod at weather. "The pharmacy machine told my husband something like that too," she said. "He said the machine was old." Ms. Warsame was watching from the doorway, arms folded, expression unreadable, and Jade could not tell whether she had done something wrong by looking it up or something right.

The rest of the morning Jade spent thinking about what she would say to Aya, which was a way of not thinking about the woman in the chair, whose filling was repaired without incident while a radio played softly overhead. Ms. Warsame, between patients, told a story about a man who'd had a stroke of luck with a molar and now liked to convalesce in the waiting room for the free coffee, telling anyone who sat down that flossing was invented by dentists to sell floss. "People believe what lets them keep their habits," Ms. Warsame said. "You'll see." Jade wrote that down too, though she wasn't sure yet what to do with it.

At lunch she called Aya from the back step. "The reading was elevated," she said. "The woman's. And I didn't know what that meant, so I looked it up in the cabinet. I'm not going to pretend I knew." There was a pause long enough that Jade could hear the cafeteria behind her. Then Aya said, "Email me the sheet? There's a whole unit on this second semester," and Jade understood that Aya's want and her own were not the same want, but could still share a reference sheet, a phone call, a Wednesday.

She went back inside and asked Ms. Warsame, as casually as she could manage, whether the woman's appointment card could include a note to see her regular doctor about the reading. Ms. Warsame considered it. "Write it in the chart," she said. "I'll flag it. She may ignore it, machines being old and all. Or she may not." Jade sat down at the little intake desk and printed, in her neatest hand, the numbers and the word elevated, and set the card where it would be handed over with the receipt.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
The bus smelled of wet coats and diesel, and Noemie had the seat behind the driver to herself until Justice dropped into it at the second stop, holding a battered paperback like a piece of evidence. "Gallagher assigned the passage," Justice said. "Catherine deciding to marry Edgar instead of Heathcliff. We have to say whether her choice is her own or whether it's what her society trained her to want." The paper cover had gone soft at the corners, and Noemie took it and read the same paragraph she'd read three times the night before, the one where Catherine says she'd be degraded by marrying Heathcliff, that it would change and degrade her.

"She wants money and status," Noemie said. "So she's greedy. That's an interpretation."

"That's a verdict," Justice said. "Interpretations are harder."

At the back of the bus, Clark was arguing with two boys about the hockey game, loud, confident, the kind of confidence that filled a whole row. He noticed the book and leaned over the seat. "Wuthering Heights? My mom read that in her book club. They fought about it for a month." He grinned. "You should've heard them. It was like a divorce proceeding."

Noemie remembered, then, the winter her grandmother had come to convalesce at their house after her surgery, installed on the living room sofa with a stack of library books like a small fortress. Noemie had been twelve and bored, and her grandmother, a taciturn woman who rationed her words as carefully as her pills, had once handed her a thick blue book without explanation. Noemie had read a page at random, understood nothing, and asked what it was. Her grandmother had said only, "Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, 1949," and gone back to her reading, as though that were the whole answer. It had taken Noemie until this morning to understand that it might have been.

She hadn't found the book again until last night, in a box her mother was donating.
