She'd sat on her bedroom floor with it, working through a chapter, and one line had stopped her completely: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. She'd read it four times. She'd written it on her wrist, where the ink was still faintly visible under her sleeve, and she had not told anyone, not even Justice, because she wasn't sure yet what she had.

"Is that ink?" Justice asked, squinting at her wrist.

Noemie pulled her sleeve down. "It's nothing. A reminder."

"You're hoarding again. You do this. You found something and you're sitting on it like a dragon."

The bus lurched around the corner by the pharmacy and everyone slid sideways. Clark caught the book before it hit the floor. "My mom's club had this whole fight," he said, "about whether Catherine was a victim of her time or just a person making a bad call. Half of them said you can't blame her, the other half said that's letting her off easy. And this one guy kept quoting this French woman until they made him stop."

"What French woman?" Noemie asked, though her pulse had picked up, though she already half knew.

"I don't know. Simone something. He'd do this thing with his glasses." Clark pushed imaginary glasses up his nose, and Justice laughed so hard she knocked her water bottle off the seat, and even Noemie laughed, watching the bottle roll down the aisle while the driver called out about feet out of the aisle, please.

She turned the paperback over in her hands. Catherine's choice looked different now, but not simpler. If a girl wasn't born a woman but became one, then every want Catherine had, even her love for Heathcliff, even her love for money, had been shaped by a world that measured women by whom they married. That didn't make the choice meaningless. It made it hers and not hers at the same time, and Noemie couldn't find a sentence for that, and Gallagher wanted five hundred words by Thursday.

"Okay," she said finally, and rolled up her sleeve so Justice could see the inked line. "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Simone de Beauvoir, The Second Sex, 1949." She watched Justice's face change. "My grandmother gave it to me years ago and I ignored it. So Catherine isn't born wanting Edgar's money. She's trained into it. But here's what I can't figure out." She tapped the paragraph. "If everything she wants was taught to her, how do we tell a real choice from a trained one? Can we? Ever?"

Justice was quiet for a stop and a half, which was a record. "Maybe you say that," Justice said slowly. "Maybe that's the honest answer. That the lens shows you the cage and not the bird."

"That's actually good. Don't tell anyone you said that."

Clark leaned over again, handing back the water bottle. "For the record, my mom's club never solved it either. They just switched to a wine night."

The bus slowed at the school loop. Noemie closed the paperback, kept her thumb in the page, and stood up with the line still drying slightly smudged on her wrist. "Write it down before you forget," she told Justice. "The cage and the bird. I'm stealing it for Thursday."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The recipe card in Hayden's hand was his grandmother's, written in pencil gone soft with age, and it said seven minutes for the pasta. He set the big pot on the burner, filled it from the tap, and turned the dial to high, and while he waited for the water he got out the eggs and butter because the sauce came next and it frightened him more than the pasta did. His father was due home at seven. His mother was already asleep upstairs after the night shift, and somebody had to make dinner, and tonight that somebody was him.

He was making the meal as a kind of argument. The family had come back from the mountains on Sunday, and the whole trip had gone wrong in small ways that added up, and Hayden wanted to prove that the pasta fiasco had not been his fault. At the campsite, at five thousand feet, he had boiled the pasta for the seven minutes on the card and it had come out hard, chalky at the center, and his father had laughed and said Hayden couldn't cook his way out of a paper bag. Hayden had let it go at the time because you let things go with fathers, but it had sat in him all week like a swallowed stone.

His phone sat propped against the flour canister, and Makenna's voice came through the speaker while she did her Spanish homework on her own counter across town. "I'm doomed," she was saying. "The quiz is on phonetics, like how the letters actually sound, and my mouth refuses to make the rolled r. I've been practicing for an hour. My little brother thinks I'm choking."

"You just have to relax your tongue," Hayden said, cracking an egg into a bowl, separating the yolk with the shell halves the way the video had shown. "That's what the video said, anyway."

"That is not encouraging from a person whose pasta turned out crunchy."

"It wasn't my fault." He said it quickly, and then, because it was Makenna and she had earned better than quick, he slowed down. "I looked it up. Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude. At five thousand feet, where we were, it boils at about ninety-five degrees Celsius instead of a hundred. So boiled foods take longer to cook there. Seven minutes was seven minutes at sea level. We were three thousand feet up a mountain."

There was a pause on the line, then the sound of Makenna attempting the rolled r again, failing, and laughing at herself. "Okay, that's actually real. My aunt in Denver complains about it. So you're making it here to prove you can?"

"I'm making it because it's dinner," Hayden said, but they both knew that was only half true, and he didn't try to hide the other half. "And maybe a little bit to prove it."

The water took longer to reach a boil than he expected even here, long enough that he second-guessed the burner, and when it finally rolled he salted it hard, the way his grandmother's card said, "like the sea," and slid the pasta in. He set the timer for seven minutes and stood over the pot with a wooden spoon, and while he stirred he thought about how strange it was that the same water, the same pasta, the same seven minutes could come out differently depending on where in the world you stood. It seemed to destabilize something he'd always assumed was fixed, like the ground shifting a centimeter under a house that still looked level. He didn't know what to do with that except notice it.

His father came in at five to seven, hung his coat on the hook, and looked at the stove. "You're cooking," he said, neutral, which was its own small victory.

"Pasta for seven minutes," Hayden said. "Same as at the camp."

"Last time seven minutes gave us gravel."

"We were at five thousand feet. Water boils lower up there, about ninety-five degrees instead of a hundred, so things take longer. It wasn't the time, it was the place." He said it evenly, without heat, and kept stirring so he wouldn't have to watch his father's face while he decided what to do with being wrong.

His father stood there a moment, then got down two plates without a word, which was its own kind of answer. When the timer went off Hayden fished out a piece of pasta and bit it, and it was done, soft all the way through, and something in his chest unclenched. He made the sauce next, whisking the egg yolks with butter over low heat, terrified the whole time that the heat would ruin it, and it came out glossy and yellow, and his father ate two helpings and said, "Your grandmother would've been proud," and then, "Next time we go up, we'll just boil it longer." Not sorry, exactly. Fathers didn't say sorry in words. But longer, at altitude, was close enough, or at least closer than they had been on Sunday, and Hayden decided he could live with not knowing exactly how close.

After dinner he called Makenna back. "It worked," he said. "Perfect pasta, perfect sauce."

"Say that again," she said. "Say it with the r's." And she made him repeat, "perfect pasta," three times, coaching him through the r's while the pot soaked in the sink, and on the third try his tongue finally rolled.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Homophily, a term from sociologists Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton in 1954, is the tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves.
story:
The cafeteria at Kingsley High had the geography of a country she had no map for. Alicia stood in the lunch line on her third day and told herself she didn't care, which was mostly true, or true the way a receipt is true until you read the fine print. She'd told her mother that leaving Riverside meant nothing, that she and Priya and Kelsey would text every night and it would be like nothing changed. That had lasted four nights.

The tables sorted themselves with an efficiency that impressed her, in a grim way. Band kids near the windows. A huddle of gamers who'd colonized the corner by the vending machines, controllers out even at lunch. Athletes in the middle like a landmass. She understood the logic of it immediately, and that was the problem: understanding a system is not the same as having a place in it. She took her tray to the end of a table occupied by a girl reading a worn paperback, and the girl glanced up, nodded once, and went back to her page. That was the whole conversation. Alicia ate pretending to be deeply interested in her milk carton.

In Mr. Novák's sociology elective, which she'd signed up for only because it fit her schedule, he'd written a word on the board on Monday and then, maddeningly, left it there without comment while he took attendance. Homophily. When a boy named Nathaniel asked what it meant, Mr. Novák only said, "Look it up, and look at who it names," and moved on to the syllabus. Alicia had done the reading that night, half-heartedly, in the empty kitchen while her mother worked late. Two sociologists, Paul Lazarsfeld and Robert Merton, coined it in 1954. The tendency of people to form ties with others similar to themselves. She'd read it twice, closed the laptop, and thought: well, obviously. Then she'd thought about Kelsey, who liked everything Alicia liked, and Priya, who liked everything Alicia hated but hated it in the same voice Alicia did, and she'd had to put her head down on the cool counter for a minute.

By Thursday she'd developed a theory, which she explained to Deshawn in fourth period because he was the only person who'd spoken to her twice and she'd decided, therefore, that he was her friend. "It's like bird migration or something," she said. "Everybody here found their similar people in September of ninth grade, and the routes are set, and I'm a bird that showed up in October of senior year."

"Homophily," Deshawn said. "Lazarsfeld and Merton, 1954. Novák made us memorize it." He didn't look up from the worksheet. "It's about people, not birds."

"Same principle."

"Maybe." He shaded in a bubble. "Or maybe you just don't want to sit with anyone who doesn't already know you."

She'd laughed at that, because it was rude, and then she hadn't laughed, because it kept ringing in her ears through lunch, through the afternoon, through the whole drive home past the strip malls of a town she still couldn't navigate without the GPS. It was a fair thing to say to someone who had, that very lunch period, watched a girl at the paperback table gesture at the empty seat across from her, and who had pretended not to see it because the girl was reading science fiction and Alicia read literary fiction and had decided, somewhere in the animal part of her brain, that this constituted a difference too large to bridge.

The truth, which Alicia was slow in handing over even to herself, was that she had rejected four people that week. A boy who talked about lacrosse too long. A girl in her stats class who was friendly but chewed with her mouth open. Two sophomores who'd invited her to a club meeting on Thursday, which she'd skipped in favor of sitting in the library texting Priya, who had replied two hours later with a string of hearts and a photo of a party Alicia hadn't been invited to, because Priya hadn't thought of her when the invite went around, because Priya had already found her replacement similar people, the way water finds a drain.

On Friday, Mr. Novák returned their first assignments, and he paused at Alicia's desk long enough to set her paper down with a grade she was proud of and to say, in the mild voice he used when he was being quietly irascible, "You write well about Riverside. You write nothing about here." She wanted to argue that the assignment had been about community, and Riverside was her community, and there was nothing underhanded about that. But he'd already moved on, and his implication hung there, unearned and yet impossible to exonerate herself from: that her nostalgia had become a kind of complicity, that she was curating her own loneliness and then billing it as fate.

That afternoon she sat with the paperback girl, whose name was not Alicia's business for the first eleven minutes and then was: Thea, or rather not Thea, because there was no Thea, because Alicia made her up on the walk to the table, rehearsed an opener, and then lost her nerve at the last second and asked, out loud, the actual question she'd been circling all week. "Is that seat taken?" The actual girl, whose name turned out to be Mara, moved her bag. She was rereading a book for the fourth time. Alicia had read one book four times in her life. She said so. Mara said, "Which one?" and it turned out to be a different one, and they argued about the endings for the rest of lunch, pleasantly, the argument itself a kind of similar taste.

She texted Priya that night anyway. Sat on her bed with the phone in both hands, typed and deleted, typed again. homophily, lazarsfeld and merton, 1954. its this thing im learning. about how people like people like them. Priya replied the next morning with a thumbs up, and Alicia stared at it for a long time, trying to decide whether it meant everything was fine or everything was already over. She left for school without deciding. At lunch, Mara had saved her a seat, and Alicia, sliding in across from her, noticed she still kept her phone face-up on the table, screen lit, waiting.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The key signature of G major has one sharp, F-sharp, which applies to every F in the piece unless an accidental changes it.
story:
The piano at his grandmother's house had not been tuned since before Eric was born, and he had begun to think of its particular flatness as a feature, the way other people thought of weather. He set his notebook on the music stand, opened it to the staff paper Mr. Qureshi had photocopied for the whole class, and looked at the sixteen bars he had written the night before. The assignment was due Monday. It was Saturday.

He had written the key signature himself, one sharp on the F line, because Mr. Qureshi had made them copy it onto every page until their hands did it without asking. G major. Then Eric had composed the melody in his head on the bus, humming it against the window, and written it down fast, before it dissolved. It had sounded good on the bus. It sounded wrong now. He played it through on the untuned piano, and at bar three something soured, and again at bar seven, and at eleven so badly that he stopped and sat with his hands in his lap like a man awaiting sentencing.

His grandmother came in with tea he had not asked for and set it on the coaster far from the piano, which was her way of being present without interfering. "You keep playing the same wrong bit," she said. "I've counted four times."

"I know," Eric said. "I just don't know why it's wrong."

She drifted back toward the kitchen, and he leaned into the keys again. Bar three. The melody climbed to an F, and the F sat there sounding like a stranger at a party who had wandered into the wrong house. He played the note alone. He played the note before it, then the F, then the note after. It was the F. Every time the tune went to F, it went wrong, and he could not understand why, because F was a perfectly legal note. It had its own line and its own space on the staff. He had written it correctly.

He thought of Anthony, who had defended his own composition in class on Thursday by saying that dissonance was intentional, and Mr. Qureshi saying, "That's a bold claim for a boy whose dynamics are all forte." Anthony grinned like a misanthrope who had found a way to get paid for it. Eric missed that classroom, suddenly, the way you miss a place only once you are alone in a quiet house with an untuned piano and a problem.

He looked at the melody again. In his head, on the bus, he had heard the tune lift at bar three. Up, not just sideways. He hummed it. Up. He looked at what he had written. He had written the F on the same line where the sharp sat in the key signature, and he had a sudden cold suspicion, so he played the black key above F instead.

It was right. It was exactly, unmistakably right, the note the bus had been humming all along. He played bar three, then seven, then eleven, finding every F and lifting it to the sharp, and the melody stopped sounding like a stranger and started sounding like itself.

He sat back. So that was what the key signature was doing at the front of every line, sitting there like a memo nobody read: it applied to every F in the piece, all sixteen bars, unless you went out of your way to cancel it. He had treated it as decoration, a piece of paperwork, when it had been an instruction the entire time. He laughed once, out loud, in the empty parlour, and heard it come back off the floral wallpaper.

"Fixed?" his grandmother called from the kitchen.

"Sort of," he called back. "I forgot something I already knew."

Last summer, before any of this, he had sat on this same bench while his grandfather played. That was the flashback that arrived now, uninvited: his grandfather's hands, spotted and enormous, moving through something slow while Eric watched and thought the notes looked like birds settling on wires. "You have to play it, not just write it," his grandfather had said, without stopping, in the tone of a man who considered recording technology anachronistic and possibly immoral. Eric had nodded and not understood. He was never going to nod at that sentence again without understanding it.

He took out a pencil. The notation itself was still right, technically, because the key signature did the work for him, but he did not trust himself anymore, so he penciled a small sharp in front of each F anyway, his own accidentals stacked on top of the rule, a belt over the suspenders. He played the whole sixteen bars through, and the melody undulated the way he had meant it to, rising and settling, and when he finished his grandmother was standing in the doorway with a dish towel over her shoulder, listening.

"That one," she said. "Play that one again."

He put his fingers back on the keys and started at bar one.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: The US ESIGN Act, passed in 2000, says a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it is in electronic form.
story:
Victor had been standing at the gym's front desk for six minutes, and the tablet on the counter had been staring back at him for five. The membership agreement glowed on the screen, all of it, forty-one pages he was supposed to scroll through before drawing his finger along a line marked SIGNATURE. He wanted the membership the way you want something you've already half imagined: the Thursday pickup games, the reason to leave the house that wasn't school or errands. His mother had said fine, but read what you're signing, which was easy for her to say. She read contracts for a living and called the fine print "the part where they keep you."

"Page one," said Fanny, who worked the desk on Saturdays and had watched him not scroll twice already. "Terms and conditions. You agree to them, they agree to let you sweat on their machines."

"I'm reading them."

"You're transfixed by them. That's different. Reading involves movement."

He was, in fairness, transfixed. Section 4 released the gym from liability for essentially everything short of the ceiling falling in, and there was a clause about consent to photographs that seemed to cover any image of him taken anywhere on the premises, forever, for purposes of promotion. He scrolled. Somewhere around page nine the words stopped meaning things and became a weather pattern, dense and gray. He looked up. "If I just drag my finger, does that count? Like legally?"

Fanny shrugged. "People do it all day."

That was not an answer, and Victor knew the difference, because his mother had drilled it into him: lots of people doing a thing is not the same as a thing being binding. He dragged his finger anyway, crooked and slow, and the tablet accepted it with a cheerful chime that felt, given the forty-one pages, like laughter at his expense.

Mr. Walker came out of the back office holding a paper form and a pen. He was the weekend manager, a broad man who had once played college ball and mentioned it in the way other people mentioned the weather. "Victor, right? There's a problem with your waiver. The system kicked it back."

"My signature?"

"Your e-signature." Mr. Walker set the paper down like a solution. "Look, the electronic thing is for convenience, but for the liability waiver we need ink. A judge isn't going to care about a finger-swipe on a screen. If you're under eighteen we need the real thing."

Victor picked up the pen, and then he didn't write, because something snagged in him, the same snag he felt when a teacher said "everyone knows." He took out his phone. "One second." Fanny leaned on the counter to see the screen, which meant Mr. Walker also had to pretend not to see the screen, and so all three of them were arranged around the little rectangle like people reading a shared letter.

The law was not hard to find. Victor read it twice, then a third time with his thumb hovering over the words, and felt the peculiar satisfaction of a fact arriving exactly when you needed it. "The ESIGN Act," he said. "Passed in 2000. It says a signature or contract may not be denied legal effect solely because it's in electronic form." He looked up. "Solely because. So it counts. The finger thing counts."

Mr. Walker's jaw moved the way it did during disputes with referees. "That's about contracts, son. A waiver's different."

"It says signature or contract." Victor kept his voice level, which took effort, because the argument was making his pulse do something gymnastic. "I'm not saying you're wrong about everything. Maybe there's a parent-consent rule for minors, I don't actually know that part. But the reason you gave, that electronic doesn't count at all, that part isn't right." It occurred to him, saying it, that he was doing the thing his mother did, holding one piece of certainty inside a larger region of honest doubt, and that he liked it, and that it was terrifying.

There was a silence in which Fanny very deliberately straightened a stack of class schedules. Then Mr. Walker laughed, one short bark, not entirely warm but not hostile either. "You want the paper anyway?" He slid the form forward. "Consider it a workout for your wrist."

Victor signed the paper, in ink, his name suddenly formal and unfamiliar in cursive. Then, because the tablet still showed his crooked finger-swipe on its confirmation page, he asked Fanny to print a copy of that too. "Both," he said. "Redundant is fine with me." She printed it and stamped it with the date, and he folded the two documents into his back pocket, where they made a stiff square against his leg like a small, negotiable promise.

The gym smelled of rubber and disinfectant, and beyond the desk the courts were already loud with a Saturday game. Mr. Walker watched him stand there, holding a pen he'd forgotten to hand back. "You start today, or you going home to read those?"

"Both of those things can be true," Victor said, and pushed through the turnstile.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those observed if there were truly no effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
story:
Olivier had until Friday to turn in the review, and by Wednesday lunch he had written two paragraphs that said almost nothing. The assignment was to compare two scholarly articles on the same question, and Mr. Cheung had approved his choice with unsettling enthusiasm: one study claimed that listening to music while studying improved recall, and a second, larger study found no effect at all. Two articles, one question, opposite answers, and Olivier had to say something considered about both.

He had spread the papers across a table in the library annex, the good table by the window, when Iyad dropped into the chair across from him and stole a pretzel from the bag Olivier had been rationing.

"Still fighting the music thing?" Iyad asked. He picked up the first article and read the abstract with the showy confidence of someone skimming. "Okay, so this one says it works. Ninety-five percent. That's basically proven, right?"

"That's what I wrote at first," Olivier said. "That the study was ninety-five percent likely to be right."

Iyad looked up. "Isn't it? That's what the number means?"

Olivier turned the paper around and tapped the sentence he had underlined three times, the one with the p-value in it, the little number sitting at the end of a long statistical sentence he had avoided for two days. "I don't think so. I've read this paragraph four times. It says the p-value is the probability of getting results at least as extreme as those they got if there were truly no effect. Not the probability that the hypothesis is true."

Iyad frowned at the page. "Those sound like the same thing."

"They're not, though. It's like, the chance of the evidence showing up if the music does nothing. It's a statement about the evidence, not about the truth." Olivier heard himself say it and felt the ground shift slightly, the way it did in chemistry when enthalpy had finally stopped being a word on a worksheet and become a thing he could picture, energy folded inside a reaction waiting to be accounted for. "So my sentence was wrong. Like, backwards wrong."

"Congrats," Iyad said, taking another pretzel. "You have to rewrite it by Friday."

That was the problem, and Olivier sat with it for a moment before pulling his laptop over. The rewrite meant more than fixing one sentence. If the p-value wasn't a probability of truth, then the whole shape of his review had to change. He couldn't just crown the first study the winner and bury the second. He reread the second article's methods section, then the first one's, and noticed something he had been circling without seeing: the first study had fifty-two participants, all from one psychology course, all volunteers; the second had over eight hundred, drawn from several schools. The first had a small p-value and a fragile sample. The second had a null result on a foundation like poured concrete.

He started typing in the sudden, slightly sweaty way of someone who has found the shape of an argument and is afraid of losing it. The two studies weren't just disagreeing, he wrote; they were asking compatible questions with incompatible tools. The first showed that an effect could appear under those conditions in that group. The second showed that it didn't hold at scale. A careful reader didn't have to pick a champion. He stopped, reread that, and made himself be circumspect: he added a clause admitting that the second study could also be missing something real but small, and that his conclusion was about which evidence was stronger, not about which claim was true. He didn't love the admission. It felt like leaving a door open in a house he was trying to close. But the sentence was honest, and Mr. Cheung had written "don't suture the disagreement shut too early, let it breathe" in the margin of his last essay, a comment Olivier had found baffling until now.

At eleven that night, he was still adjusting the paragraph where the two perspectives met, trying to make the joining feel like a real thought instead of a diplomatic shrug. His mother came by with tea and read a paragraph over his shoulder, which he allowed because she had been circumspect about his drafts since the incident in grade ten, when he had thrown a history essay in the recycling. "So which one is right?" she asked.

"Neither of them is right," he said. "That's not the question they answer."

"They answer a question?"

"Everything answers a question. You just have to find out which one." He saved the document, checked the time, and decided the conclusion could wait until morning.

Friday, Mr. Cheung handed the essays back in reverse alphabetical order, which meant Olivier waited through the whole period watching everyone else read their margins. When his finally arrived, the grade was fine, better than fine, but that wasn't the thing he stared at. Under his carefully hedged conclusion, where he had admitted he couldn't say whether music truly helped, Mr. Cheung had written: "Correct instinct. The original authors would agree with you. See their reply paper, 2019, in the same journal, where they concede the sampling problem themselves."

Olivier laughed out loud, then covered his mouth. The researchers had beaten him to his own conclusion by four years.

Iyad leaned over from the next row. "What?"

"I was being original," Olivier whispered, "and it turns out I was being late."

He flipped to the citation, copied it onto the inside cover of his notebook, and put a star beside it for the next essay.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Under the US Help America Vote Act of 2002, a voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot, which counts only once officials confirm eligibility.
story:
Nicole arrived at the community hall twenty minutes after the polls opened, before her first class, with her driver's license in the front pocket of her jacket where she could feel it against her chest. The line undulated down the steps and out toward the parking lot, parents with toddlers on their hips, an old man with a folding cane, two of her classmates from economics, Shyla and Summer, waving her over. Nicole had turned eighteen in March, five weeks before the registration deadline, and she had filled out the form at the DMV counter while the clerk waited with her hand out for the next document. She had checked the box. She remembered checking the box.

Inside, the folding tables had been pushed together under the basketball hoops, and a laptop sat where the scoreboard controls used to be. A poll worker with reading glasses on a chain found her street, then ran a finger down the column twice. "You're not in here, honey." Nicole said that couldn't be right, and gave her date of birth, and spelled her last name with the accent over nothing, plain eight letters. The finger ran down again. Behind her, someone shifted their weight and sighed.

"There's another option," the worker said. "It's called a provisional ballot. Under the Help America Vote Act, if your eligibility is in question, you can still vote. It goes in a separate envelope, and it counts only once the officials confirm you're eligible." Nicole said yes before the sentence was finished, and the worker went to fetch the envelope from a cardboard box labeled with masking tape.

Shyla appeared beside her, having already voted, the "I Voted" sticker on her collar like a name tag. "What happened?" Nicole told her, keeping her voice even, and Shyla said, "We registered the same week. I did mine online." Nicole had not known there was an online form. She had stood at the DMV and done what was in front of her. She filled out the provisional envelope at a side table, printed her address, signed her name twice, and the worker sealed it in front of her and set it in a tray with two others. It looked like very little, a white envelope in a plastic tray.

She walked to class through the parking lot, and it occurred to her that she did not know what happened to the envelope next, or when, or whom she would ask. She had a political science seminar that afternoon, and the instructor, a laconic man who assigned Supreme Court opinions and said almost nothing about them, put the question to the room: what does it mean to cast a vote that may or may not be counted? Someone said it was a placeholder, someone said it was a promise the state had to keep, and Nicole, who almost never spoke, said that hers was sitting in a tray at the community hall and she had no idea which of those it was.

After class she called the county election office from the bench outside the gym. The man who answered asked for her name and date of birth, and keyboard sounds followed. He said the DMV transmission had come through incomplete for a batch of registrations in the spring, and that hers showed a missing signature page. He said she could come in within the week with her license and sign the page, and then the ballot would be reviewed like any other. She wrote the address on the back of her hand. She asked whether it would count by the time the results were announced, and he said he couldn't promise that, only that it would be processed correctly.

She was quiet that evening at dinner, and her mother asked how the voting had gone. "It went," Nicole said. Her mother said she remembered the form, remembered Nicole standing at the counter with the pen that barely wrote, and Nicole cut her off, not unkindly, and said it wasn't anyone's fault, it was a missing page in a stack somewhere. Her mother said that seemed like a lot of ceremony for something so small, and Nicole said the ceremony was the part she could see; the rest of it, the counting, the confirming, happened where nobody was watching. That had been the strange discovery of the day, that voting was two things at once, a private act in a booth and an administrative fact in a file, and she had only ever been promised the first one.

Two days later she signed the page at the county office, a counter like the DMV counter, a clerk who did not look up. On the drive back she passed the community hall, its folding tables visible through the window being stacked against the wall, the banners still up, the gym returned to its ordinary purpose after the brief interregnum when it had been something else. She slowed down going past. There was no way to know yet whether her envelope had been opened, whether her marks had joined the marks of Shyla and Summer and the man with the folding cane. She parked, got out, and stood for a minute on the steps where the line had been. Then she took the sticker off her jacket, the one she had kept in her pocket, and pressed it onto her sleeve.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The cultural center smelled of sesame oil and paper dust, and Kate stood in the doorway with her mother's tupperware of mandarin oranges balanced against her hip, looking for a table that wasn't already full. The hall had been decorated since morning: red lanterns strung along the ceiling fans, a calligraphy banner she couldn't read, and a table near the stage where two women were stacking small red envelopes into tidy towers. Kate watched them work. She was eighteen now, and for the first time in her life she wasn't sure whether the envelopes were for her.

"Kate! Over here." Aliyah was waving from the volunteer table, wearing the same borrowed red scarf she'd worn last year. She was sorting donation receipts with the brisk, unbothered efficiency of someone who had already decided the evening would go well. "Rosemarie's coming at seven, after her shift. Ms. Lawson brought her whole math department, can you believe it. They took the table by the kitchen."

"Does Ms. Lawson even celebrate?" Kate set down the oranges.

"She said the center isn't sectarian, it's communal, whatever that means. She's been here every year since we were freshmen." Aliyah squinted at the towers of envelopes across the hall. "Go ask Auntie Ying for your envelope before the line gets long."

"It's fine," Kate said, and heard how flat it came out. "I'm eighteen. I have a debit card. I pay for my own bus fare."

Aliyah looked at her the way she looked at a proof that had gone wrong in step two. "That's not how it works."

But Kate didn't ask how it worked, because her mother was already beckoning from the food line, and because she wasn't sure she wanted the answer. Somewhere between childhood and this evening, the envelope had become a question. She was leaving for college in the fall, eight hours away, and part of her wanted to arrive there already finished, already someone who gave rather than received. She carried the oranges to the kitchen and tried to stop thinking about it.

She found Ms. Lawson by the tea urns, filling a paper cup with the concentration of a woman who took all activities seriously. "Kate. Are you enjoying the celebration?" It wasn't small talk with Ms. Lawson; it was a genuine inquiry, the kind she aimed at her calculus students. When Kate hesitated, Ms. Lawson tilted her head. "Something's on your mind. You have the look of a student stuck on a lemma. You know, the small stepping-stone problem you have to solve before the real one."

Kate laughed despite herself. "It's a small problem. Honestly it's stupid."

"I've never met a stupid problem, only unadmitted ones."

"The red envelopes," Kate said. "I don't know if I still get one. I'm not a kid anymore. And I can't exactly ask my grandmother, because if the answer is no, I'd have to watch her realize it at the same moment I do."

Ms. Lawson sipped her tea and said nothing, which was her way of returning the problem to its owner. Kate appreciated that about her. She appreciated it even more an hour later, when Rosemarie finally arrived, smelling of the coffee shop where she worked, and dragged Kate toward the stage where the older relatives were gathering.

"Grandmother Chen is giving them out," Rosemarie said. "Come on. Last year you got one and I got one and we spent it on bubble tea, remember?"

"I remember. But Rosemarie, we're eighteen."

"So? My cousin got them until she was twenty-four. She said it's for children and unmarried younger relatives, so as long as you're not married, you count." Rosemarie said it the way she reported everything, as a fact she had collected and was now delivering free of charge. "My cousin's wedding was in June. This is her first year giving instead of getting. She cried about it, actually. A little."

Kate stood near the back of the line, watching Grandmother Chen work. The old woman pressed each envelope into a pair of hands with the same deliberate care, and when one of the small boys tried to open his immediately, his mother caught his fingers and shook her head. "Not yet," the mother murmured. "Say thank you first." The red of the envelopes was the same red as the lanterns, the same red as the scarves, so saturated it seemed to hum under the fluorescent lights.

When Kate's turn came, Grandmother Chen held the envelope out, and Kate hesitated, one heartbeat, two, and the old woman said, "Take it. Red is for good fortune. Red keeps the evil away." She pressed it into Kate's palm and closed Kate's fingers around it with both of her own, her hands cool and light as paper. "You go far away next year. You take the red with you."

Kate said thank you, in the language her mother had drilled into her and which she usually mangled, and stepped aside into the noise of the hall, the envelope warm in her hand even though it was only paper and a folded bill. She still didn't know the exact age when it stopped, or whether wanting it made her younger or just honest, and she found she could hold all of that at once, the uncertainty sitting beside the certainty of the red in her palm. Rosemarie appeared at her elbow.

"So," Rosemarie said. "Bubble tea?"

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal.
story:
Sophia spread the two articles across the kitchen table and weighted their corners with the salt shaker and her mother's teacup, which was still warm. The question both papers addressed was whether social media use makes teenagers more anxious, and her assignment, the first real one of the semester, was to write a critical review comparing them. Article A had appeared in a journal with a long name and a long history; Article B had a brighter, punchier argument, the kind her father would have called common sense if her father were speaking to her this week. She read them again with a pen in her hand and felt the pleasing click of two positions lining up against each other, ready to be weighed.

Then she turned to the first page of Article B and looked, really looked, at where it had come from. There was no journal name. There was a server she didn't recognize, a posting date, and a banner across the top of the PDF that she had skimmed past twice.

She texted Mohammed, who had done the same assignment last year for Ms. Lim. "Article B isn't from a journal. It says preprint."

He called her within a minute, out of breath from the stairs. "A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review," he said. "So its findings haven't been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal. Not yet, anyway."

"So it's not real."

"It's real, it's just not vetted. Ms. Lim failed a guy in my class for treating them the same. Or she didn't fail him, she just wrote 'so what?' in the margin about forty times."

Sophia hung up and sat with the two papers, tapping the pen against her teeth. The preprint was the one she had liked. Its author argued that platforms deliberately commodify teenage attention, packaging insecurity into a product that could be sold, and the prose had a heat to it that the journal article, careful and hedged and dull, entirely lacked. The journal paper found a small effect, hedged it further, and concluded with a paragraph of caveats so thick it seemed to apologize for existing.

Karim arrived at four with the good cookies and no intention of working, but he let himself be pulled down into a chair. "Which one's right?" he asked, stealing the pen.

"That's the wrong question, apparently."

"Then what's the right question?"

She laid the papers side by side. "The preprint says the effect is huge. The journal one says it's small and depends on the kid. The preprint hasn't been checked by anyone. The journal one has. But the preprint might still be onto something, because peer review doesn't mean true, it means checked." She heard herself say it and tested it against what Mohammed had told her, and it held. "So maybe the honest review is that the strong claim is unverified and the weak claim is boring but survives scrutiny, and I have to say what I'd trust and why."

"Sounds like a recipe for a C," Karim said, mouth full. "Just pick the strong one. Teachers like confidence."

"Ms. Lim does not like confidence. She wrote on my last essay that I sounded like an ideologue, which I had to look up, and which was, honestly, gratuitous." She winced at her own sentence even as she said it. "She was right about the first word, anyway."

He laughed, then turned quiet in the way that meant he was actually thinking. "So what would you trust? If it were your little sister asking."

Sophia looked at the table. The teacup had gone cold; the salt shaker still held the preprint's corner down like a small paperweight on an argument that hadn't earned its weight. She thought of her cousin, eleven years old, who had stopped eating lunch at school because of something that happened in a group chat, and of the journal paper's careful graphs, which would never once mention a girl alone at a cafeteria table.

"Both," she said. "The checked one for what's likely. The unchecked one for what's possible and worth checking." She pulled a fresh page toward her and wrote at the top, in handwriting she would later cringe at for its neatness: These articles disagree not only about findings but about what counts as knowing. She underlined it, then thought better of the underline and left it, a small stripe of conviction she couldn't entirely defend.

Karim read over her shoulder. "That's actually not bad."

"Write your own essay," she said, and moved the salt shaker off the good cookies.
